news.title: ‘The View’ co-hosts say Dems shouldn’t impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress
news.text:
“The View” co-hosts agreed with former Vice President Kamala Harris Friday that impeachment would not be a good use of the Democratic Party’s time and resources if the party wins back control of Congress in the midterm elections.

“I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris warned Tuesday on “The Parnas Perspective” podcast. “OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that’s where the time should be spent. Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren’t there, right? So, that’s how I feel.”

After playing a clip of Harris’ comments, “The View” co-hosts agreed with her assessment.

“In terms of Trump, no, I don’t think that’s what should be on the agenda,” co-host Sunny Hostin said. “Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades. 

“And then he’s got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump.”

“I think that Democrats have to be realistic of what’s achievable,” co-host Ana Navarro said. “We are four days away from the election. So, before we start talking about what Democrats are going to do once they win, they’ve got to make sure they win. 

“People have to focus not on all of the conversation about impeachment and what is going to happen but rather on getting out the vote and getting people to the polls so that the American people decide who they want in power in the House and in the Senate.

“There’s a limit to what Democrats are going to be able to do even if they win the House, even if they win the House and the Senate, because Donald Trump is still president,” she continued. “Legislation in this country needs to be signed by the president. If not, it needs to have a veto-proof majority. And I think that’s going to be very difficult to achieve. I’m completely against impeachment.

“There’s 100 other ways to hold Donald Trump and his administration accountable,” Navarro added. “Impeachment is an exercise that’s moot if you don’t have the 67 votes in the Senate required to indict.”

Joy Behar pointed to former President Richard Nixon’s resignation from office after Republican lawmakers warned him that he lacked sufficient Senate support to avoid conviction if impeached and said of Trump, “If we don’t have the votes to convict, there’s no point in impeaching.”

Sara Haines also agreed, arguing that many of Trump’s supporters are now angry with him for breaking campaign promises and that Democrats could capitalize on their dissatisfaction by delivering on their own promises.

“It’s important to recognize the moment,” she said. “Donald Trump was elected and promised things he never touched. He’s been remodeling, redecorating, working to revenge, all the things. The voters were left high and dry, which is why we’re seeing some red states flip full to blue,” she said. “That’s why we are watching this campaigning.

“They need to see someone get in there, hold them accountable, do the investigations, fine,” Haines continued. “But really show the American people that what they promised, to fix all these things, that immediately there’s action taken. Even if it can’t get past the president. Spin the wheels. Show the people that you are putting up policy, that you are taking things to vote, that you are actually acting for the people that put you there.”

“Impeachment is not where the focus should be,” Alyssa Farah Griffin said. “It costs actually a lot of money to do a trial, do the investigation.

“What I think is important is there are day one things that would be beneficial for all Americans and a lot of Republicans would be on board with that a Democratic Congress could do,” she continued.

“Repealing Trump’s tariffs, that is the power of the purse controlled by Congress and trying to wind down or pause the war in Iran. Those are things you should get Republican votes to do. That will bring down people’s fuel prices. Those are where the focus should be.”

Earlier this month, veteran Democratic strategist James Carville also warned Democrats against impeaching Trump if the party wins control of Congress in the midterms.

Democratic strategist and co-host of “The Huddle” podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, “Neither the Senate arithmetic nor the American people are there. Folks are angry with the president about the economy, tariffs, healthcare, the war with Iran, corruption. They feel he is focused on everything but them.

“Our job is to fight for the real lives of real people, solving their problems, while providing appropriate oversight of the executive branch and trusting the electorate provides accountability,” he added. 

“The quickest path back to the minority or continuing to be on the outside, looking into the White House, is to focus on revenge and score settling.”
news.summary: "The View" co-hosts agreed with Kamala Harris that Democrats should focus on policy and investigations rather than impeaching President Donald Trump.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Elon Musk Warns 2028 Democratic Sweep Could Mean ‘End of Democracy’
news.text: Billionaire Elon Musk issued a stark warning to voters if Democrats sweep the chambers of Congress and the presidency in 2028, saying it could lead to the "end of democracy." Musk's message comes just four days ahead of the midterm elections, where Democrats are favored to take the House and face a competitive battle to flip the Senate. In his post to X early Friday morning, Musk laid out his three concerns. The first, he says, Democrats will make Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia states, in an effort to achieve a strong majority in the Senate. Secondly, Musk warned that Democrats would open the borders and "legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority." Lastly, Musk said Democrats would increase the size of the Supreme Court in an effort to gain an immediate majority. "This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one," Musk concluded in his post. Billionaire businessman Mark Cuban reacted to Musk's post on X saying: "I’m against all of these. The new force in politics and elections is independents. The fact independents are NOT an organized party, means we can individually do what we think is right, without regard to party politics. That is a force we have not seen before. And it is only growing as we all become increasingly disgusted by party politics. Pushing these would backfire on Democrats," Cuban said. This is not the first time the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has made a fourth quarter election warning. During the 2024 presidential election, Musk said that if President Donald Trump lost his race to then Vice President Kamala Harris, it would have been the last election for Americans due to immigration that would have turned the U.S. into a "single party country." Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3, to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates. Newsweek reached out to the White House, Musk via SpaceX, and the Democratic National Committee (DNC) by email on Friday for comment. What Democrats Have Said About Supreme Court Justices and Puerto Rico, D.C. Statehood Musk is not the first person to raise the concern of Democrats potentially expanding the Supreme Court or pushing D.C. and Puerto Rican statehood over the finish line. In April, Trump ripped into longtime political commentator James Carville over the thoughts, saying in part, "Wacko James Carville, a so-called Democrat 'strategist,' wants the Democrats to make D.C. and Puerto Rico States and, most importantly, pack the Supreme Court, putting 13 Justices on the Court. Other Dems want 21 Justices. If they pull off adding these two States, these Country Destroying Sleazebags will dominate politics in America, if we even have a Nation left, for 100 years (TERMINATE THE FILIBUSTER!)." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was asked if he supports adding more justices to the High Court earlier this year, and he responded saying that he supports reform. "What I support is dramatic reform, and what that looks like, to begin with, is making sure that the Supreme Court actually has an ethical code of conduct so that they’re not able to simply conduct themselves in ways that are inconsistent with the notion in this country that no one is above the law, " Jeffries said on NBC's Meet The Press in August. He added that Judiciary Committee Democrats will look further into what "dramatic reform" could be. Notably, Kamala Harris has previously supported the idea of adding justices to the Court and making D.C. and Puerto Rico states. “I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court,” Harris said on the Baby, This is Keke Palmer podcast this month. “We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States.” She also supported pushing for Puerto Rico and D.C. statehood if their residents want it, during the podcast. Democratic Representative Jim Clyburn of South Carolina previously said he too would support adding seats to the High Court. Lawmakers recently voted on a GOP-backed amendment to cap the Supreme Court at nine justices. The vote failed to get two-thirds support. D. Stephen Voss, political professor at the University of Kentucky, told Newsweek on Friday in part, "Expanding the number of states in a way that would improve Democratic political fortunes has long been a goal among activists on the left, although it's unclear how broadly popular such proposals would be with mainstream Democratic politicians in Congress." Democrats and Immigration As Trump's second term is well underway, Democrats have made their opposition to his administration's immigration policies known. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in major U.S. cities, deportations and fatal shootings involving federal agents have prompted Democrats to speak out in fury. Trump has made stricter border enforcement a key pillar of his presidency, including efforts to continue building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border and initially suspending asylum at the border, which has faced legal setbacks. However, numerous Democrats, including candidates in key midterm races, have hit back at President Joe Biden's handling of the border, going as far as to say he "failed us." Democrats have also called for making the path to obtain U.S. citizenship simpler while leaning into ICE as a central focus of the midterms. Democratic candidates, like Florida's Angie Nixon and Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, have called for ICE to be abolished or dismantled while advocating for a new immigration enforcement system to be built "from scratch." On its website, the DNC says in part that the party believes in "secure borders, common-sense immigration laws, and fair enforcement." "We also believe in the humanity and dignity of every person. Federal agents should not be able to take over your city, target children, or kill innocent people in the streets," the DNC added on its website. Voss later said in his response to Newsweek that, "On the other hand, the Democratic Party has not advocated either throwing open the borders or granting widespread amnesty to illegal migrants. At worst, a critic might argue that today's Democratic Party opposes most muscular policies intended to curtail immigration." How Much Money Has Musk Donated This Midterm Cycle? Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Musk spent $276 million, with a majority going to the Senate Leadership Fund, this cycle. He also donated $76 million earlier this year to his America PAC, which has backed Republicans in House and Senate races. On Friday, The Times reported the total figure of Musk's spending has risen to nearly $475 million this cycle. Newsweek cannot independently verify that figure at the time of publication. Other outlets also highlight that Musk's spending has surpassed $400 million. news.summary: Musk laid out his concerns if Democrats win the majority, while urging voters to back Republican senators in the midterms.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: Inside the Fight to Flip the Biggest Battleground in Texas
news.text:
I met up with Crystal Mason in mid-October, in a hilly neighborhood south of downtown Fort Worth. She was easy enough to recognize—she wore a black t-shirt with a pair of bright red boxing gloves on the front, and a single word in big block letters, “STILL ACQUITTED.” 

Eight years ago, amid a push by Texas Republican officials to find and prosecute instances of voter fraud, the Fort Worth resident was sentenced to five years in prison for voting in the 2016 presidential election while on supervised release for a felony conviction. Mason argued that she had never been informed she couldn’t vote, and that she cast only a provisional ballot, which was never counted. In 2024, a court agreed and threw out the conviction, but Tarrant County’s Republican district attorney appealed that decision. She finally beat the case for good this September—and then got right back to work. 

When I met her, she was checking a voter list on her phone and rattling off instructions to a group of volunteers—two daughters, a son, and one grandkid—who had accompanied her to knock doors and check in with residents on a 94-degree afternoon. These days, when she’s not driving a box truck for her day job, she runs a voting rights group called Crystal Mason: The Fight. In recent weeks she’d participated in registration drives, hit the doors, and stopped by a senior center on karaoke night to make sure voters there had a plan to get to the polls.

The kind of organizing Mason and others have been doing has taken on a new urgency ahead of the November election. In September, the Republican-led county commission eliminated 92 Election Day voting sites—nearly a third of its 2024 total. Advocates argued the reductions would disproportionately affect Black and Hispanic areas. Mason calls the closures “unreal.”

This would be a big deal anywhere, but Tarrant is not just any county; it’s the state’s ultimate battleground. The area has narrowly backed Democrats at the top of the ticket in some recent cycles, but it’s the last of the state’s big urban counties still run by Republicans—including the district attorney who tried to reinstate Mason’s conviction. And the conservative enclaves of Tarrant have played an outsized role in shaping the recent trajectory of the Texas Republican Party. This year’s Conservative Political Action Conference took place in the Fort Worth suburb of Grapevine. Bo French, the racist nominee for Texas Railroad Commission who wants to remove all Muslims from the United States, is a former Tarrant GOP chair. The True Texas Project, formerly known as the Northeast Tarrant Tea Party, celebrated its 15th anniversary by hosting a conversation on “the war on white America”; this fall, it’s held screenings of a new documentary called Don’t Sharia My Texas, at chapters around the state.

In light of the stakes and the preeminence of Tarrant County, the local Democratic Party headquarters in an office park on the edge of Fort Worth had been bustling with volunteers and candidates, as well as ink-stained wretches like me. When I spent a little too long admiring the political paraphernalia at the front of the office—including Kamala Harris-branded beer cans and a wine glass for Wendy Davis—Reyne Telles, the Tarrant County Democratic Party’s executive director, wistfully quoted the Boston Globe’s recent description of the space: “The Tarrant County Democratic Party office is a shrine to great hopes past.” 

Telles says that every statewide candidate on his side of the ledger has a number in mind for how much they need to win the county by in order to win the state—generally somewhere between three and eight percentage points. But there are some indications Democrats have made inroads, including with residents who traditionally support the other side. In a special election earlier this year, a Democratic union leader named Taylor Rehmet stunned political observers by flipping a state Senate district that had voted for Trump by 17 points. The data suggested he owed much of his success to persuasion, not turnout. While the official county Republican organization carries the flag for the far right, Fort Worth’s moderate Republican mayor, Mattie Parker, has endorsed Democratic candidates for two statewide offices—railroad commissioner (against French) and attorney general. Glen Whitley, who served for 16 years as Tarrant County judge (it’s the equivalent of county executive) cut an ad endorsing Democratic state Rep. James Talarico over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the race for US Senate. 

While Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa have captured most of the headlines (guilty), the stakes are high in Tarrant County’s local races, where Democrats have not won a countywide race in decades. Alisa Simmons, a Democratic county commissioner, is in a tight race against the incumbent county judge Tim O’Hare—a conservative Bo French ally who pushed the reduction in polling locations. 

“He’s a really interesting person—I’m not sure why he even wanted to serve because he’s not serving,” Simmons told me, before a fundraiser at a private home in Colleyville.

Good governance has been a major feature of the campaign. In 2025, even before Republicans in the state legislature redrew the state’s congressional maps, O’Hare embarked on an unusual attempt to gerrymander the county commissioner districts, in order to secure what Republicans hope will be a 4–1 majority. The commission has cut its meeting schedule in half, all guest speakers are limited to one minute, and attendees have been hauled out by sheriffs deputies for clapping. (In one notable case, a local activist who used the word “bullshit” in his testimony was charged, one week later, with disorderly conduct.) In our short conversation, Simmons took aim at the county’s Republican leaders for cutting taxes meant to fund the county hospital, and highlighted the rising death toll at Tarrant County jails. 

“We almost rival Harris County, and Harris County is double the population,” she said, referring to the jurisdiction that includes Houston.

Democrats in Tarrant believe the county is there for the taking this year—that the apathy and resignation that have kept turnout lower than other large urban counties is changing, and that the Republicans on the ballot aren’t cut out for swing-state realities. Telles told me he hoped flipping the countywide races would send a signal to other corners of the state, that if a historically Republican metro famous for its cattle drives and western culture can vote blue, they can too. Republicans have pushed voter-fraud narratives and ruthless gerrymandering to preserve their grip on power. But in doing so, they also reminded voters what was really at stake.

As we walked through Fort Worth, I suggested to Mason that the kind of ordeal she went through might have easily turned her away from politics. 

“I realized that’s exactly what they wanted me to do,” she said. “And that was to stand on display and tell them how I would never vote again to discourage the black and the brown from coming to the polls.” She had an obligation, she said, “to make sure that I let them know that these same people that did this to me are elected officials.”

Mason’s door-knocking was a strictly nonpartisan operation. She congratulated a young woman who was preparing to vote for the first time, and double-checked that she knew which precinct to stop by. But not long after, voters in select Texas ZIP codes began seeing a new ad in which James Talarico sits at a kitchen table with a familiar voting-rights activist.

“Crystal didn’t back down,” he says.“And you shouldn’t either,” Mason tells the audience.

news.title: Karoline Leavitt joins Elon Musk pushing conspiracy about Supreme Court if Democrats win in the midterms
news.text:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has joined MAGA figures in peddling Elon Musk’s conspiracy theories ahead of the midterms, including an alleged plot to change the Supreme Court that would render America a “permanent one-party state.”

As the polls are increasingly pointing to a Democratic blowout next week, Musk shared a post Friday on X listing his “biggest concern[s]” if Republicans lose control of the House, Senate, and White House in 2028. 

Musk claimed that if Democrats are successful, they will “increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority.” 

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word,” he claimed.

Leavitt, who left her White House role earlier this year to focus on her family, reshared the post to her Instagram stories and said, “This is what’s at stake. Vote.”

Some prominent Democrats have called for overhauling the Supreme Court, currently stacked in favor of the Republicans with a 6-3 conservative majority. 

For example, Rhode Island Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse proposed term limits for justices, and Rep. Jamie Raskin and former Vice President Kamala Harris have supported the idea of increasing the number of justices from nine to 13. If Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, they could put four new justices on the court and swing the majority, if the numbers increase to 13. 

Supreme Court scholars have noted that reform is unlikely. The path to overhauling the highest court in the land is complex and would likely face enormous challenges, even if the Democrats retake the House and Senate next week.

The world’s richest man also claimed that if Democrats regain power, they will “make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate,” and “open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority.”

He pushed the theories to warn his 241.5 million X followers that they could stop it from happening if they voted Republican on November 3. 

“All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029,” he said. “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election.”

“It would be game over for America,” added Musk, who sewed chaos at the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term overseeing the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency.

Other MAGA figures jumped on his post and amplified it to their supporters.

“Pay attention folks,” said the president’s son, Don Jr. 

“The most important post in the history of X right here,” said conservative commentator Benny Johnson.

Former deputy FBI director Dan Bongino simply said: “Please Read This.” 

Katie Miller, married to deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, also reshared Leavitt’s post.

In September, Republicans attempted to permanently limit the number of justices to nine but the amendment was struck down in the House.
news.summary: ‘It would be game over for America,’ said Musk, who sewed chaos overseeing the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency

news.title: Early voting jumps across Senate battlegrounds as millions more Americans vote ahead of Election Day
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance and particularly sharp increases in states hosting competitive Senate races, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data five days before Election Day.

The surge is especially pronounced in Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor's races. More than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50 percent increase.

Advance voting has also increased more than 30 percent from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83 percent.

Data comes 5 days before Election Day

The data, compiled by the AP, offers a glimpse of early voter participation five days before an election that will determine control of Congress and other key contests.

Across the country, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots, nearly 10 million more than in 2022. The figures cover 47 states and Washington, D.C., compared with 48 states and the nation's capital four years ago.

In states that provide information on voters' party affiliation, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans have cast ballots early. Those figures do not account for all early voters nationwide or indicate which candidates received their votes.

The increase comes as voters prepare to decide control of Congress two years into President Donald Trump's second term, with Republicans holding the House and the Senate.

The turnout has been Texas-sized

Voters have turned out in droves during Texas' two-week early in-person voting period, which ends Friday.

In Harris County, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022.

The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris defeated Trump by nearly 6 percentage points in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

This year, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched Senate race, while Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking reelection against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trump visited Texas earlier this week, his third trip to the state in a month.

Early voting surges across Senate battleground states

Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority in a midterm election in which the battleground map has expanded significantly, with Democrats hoping to pull off upsets in states that have long favored Republicans.

In South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83 percent compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and U.S. Senate this year.

In Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democratic Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, early voting has increased 34 percent, with roughly 83,000 more ballots cast than at the same point four years ago.

Michigan and Maine, both of which have closely watched Senate races, are also seeing increases.

In Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson, early voting is up 44 percent. Michigan has recorded roughly 409,000 more early votes than at the same point in 2022, a 32 percent increase.

Voters in Michigan approved early in-person voting in November 2022, making this the first midterm election in which it is available statewide.

news.title: Harris: Let's Pack the Court and *Cackle* Create New Blue States
news.text:
Yesterday, former Vice President Kamala Harris appeared at the NAACP “We the People” event in Atlanta. In addition to voting in next week's election, Harris said, "There's some structural work that needs to be done." What kind of structural work, you ask? The kind that would create a permanent Democrat majority. On Harris' to do list was adding four justices to the Supreme Court, creating two new blue states and getting rid of the electoral college.

There should be 13 justices.” “We need to revisit the electoral college.” They’re going to stack the court and rig the game, and they’re not hiding the ball.— Andrew Kolvet (@AndrewKolvet) October 30, 2026

news.title: Could Pete Hegseth Be Impeached? What a Democratic Midterm Win Could Mean
news.text: Growing calls to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are putting pressure on Republicans as they fight to maintain their narrow majorities in Congress ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. Historically, an unpopular president’s party loses seats in midterms. President Donald Trump’s approval ratings, combined with voter frustration over the economy, have created a difficult climate for Republicans two years after his 2024 election victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris. While a Democratic takeover of the U.S. House of Representatives is not guaranteed, gaining control of the chamber would significantly strengthen the party’s ability to pursue impeachment against Hegseth. Without Republican support, initial impeachment efforts in the current GOP-controlled House have struggled to gain traction. A House impeachment would trigger a Senate trial, where conviction and removal would require a two-thirds majority, meaning it would need backing from some Republicans. Trump, meanwhile, staunchly defended Hegseth on Thursday, insisting he has done a "great job" with his sweeping changes to the U.S. military and dismissed the demands for impeachment as "terrible." However, some Democrats have made Hegseth’s removal a top goal. Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat who serves on the House Armed Services Committee, said Sunday on CBS News' Face the Nation that ousting Hegseth from the Pentagon was his "priority number one" if Democrats retake the House. Democrats have focused their criticism on Hegseth’s handling of the Iran war and a strike campaign against suspected drug vessels that has killed at least 240 people. Meanwhile, some Republicans like Representatives Mike Rogers of Alabama and Dusty Johnson of South Dakota have expressed concern over internal friction at the Pentagon and questioned whether Hegseth’s dismissal of senior military officials has harmed readiness. Hegseth is the "lowest hanging fruit because of the animosity that seems to be both from Republican and Democratic senators and staff," an unnamed Democratic aide told CNN on Friday, though significant doubts remain about whether the Senate would ever convict him. If Democrats win the House, passing articles of impeachment becomes more plausible. Yet opinion within the party remains divided. Some lawmakers say that Democratic control would be better spent conducting high-profile oversight hearings, while others expect Trump may ultimately fire Hegseth himself. The threat of congressional action is weighing on some lawmakers. The prospect of impeachment is "probably being taken more seriously privately than people realize," a Republican House staffer told Newsweek, speaking on the condition of anonymity. The Pentagon has been contacted for comment via email. Previous Impeachment Pushes While articles of impeachment are more well-known for presidents, only two cabinet secretaries, Secretary of War William W. Belknap in 1876 and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024, have ever been impeached by the House. The articles failed in the Senate in both cases. A Democrat push in April 2026, led by Arizona Representative Yassamin Ansari, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth for alleged "high crimes and misdemeanors," largely relating to the Iran war. Ansari accused Hegseth of endangering U.S. troops, negligently handling sensitive military information, blocking Congressional oversight, politicizing the military, targeting civilians and breaking the laws of armed conflict. A final impeachment article accused Hegseth of "bringing disrepute upon the United States and its armed forces." The articles haven't reached a House vote. Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican who has been openly critical of Hegseth, said in mid-September he was forcing a House vote on impeachment using a privileged measure. Massie claimed Hegseth has contravened several provisions of the 1973 War Powers Resolution and brought eight articles of impeachment against him. Among those articles, Massie accused Hegseth of "unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers." The U.S. government has said it is in an "armed conflict" with drug cartels, insisting the campaign against alleged small drug vessels in the southern Caribbean and Eastern Pacific is necessary to save American lives. Experts and many lawmakers have criticized the strikes as illegal under international law. Congressional scrutiny of the attacks tightened after it emerged U.S. forces killed survivors of the first attack in September 2025 with a follow-up strike. Both sets of impeachment articles this year were seen as a long shot, and House Speaker Mike Johnson quickly recessed the chamber without a vote on Massie's measure taking place—meaning Republicans did not have to pass public judgement on Hegseth's leadership of the Pentagon ahead of the midterms. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat—a potential speaker waiting in the wings should the House be flipped—has skirted around the question, suggesting to MS NOW on Saturday instead the Democrats would hold Hegseth "accountable in the same way" as former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem. The two were both fired by Trump, rather than chased out by articles of impeachment. "Hegseth needs to be pushed aside by the president, or we’re going to have to deal with that situation if he is not," Jeffries told MS NOW. And the suggestion of impeachment has gathered pace among some outspoken Republicans. Massie told the Responsible Statecraft magazine last month Congress has "exhausted every other remedy to make things right." Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, meanwhile, has described voting to confirm Hegseth in his role nearly two years ago as the "biggest regret" of his career. "He needs to go," Tillis, who didn't run for reelection this year, told reporters last month. "Whether it's impeachment or the most expedient route—it's just the president would replace him—would be great." Another avenue for the Democrats could be threatening to hold up the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which was pushed through the House in July but has since languished in the Senate, unless Hegseth is removed. The NDAA, which sets out the Pentagon's priorities and authorized its spending, is a "must-pass" piece of legislation. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Federica Bindi.
news.summary: President Trump has defended Hegseth, insisting he has done a "great job" and dismissed the demands for impeachment as "terrible."
news.author: Ellie Cook

news.title: Four compete for two Republican-held House seats in Dublin, Jaffrey, Rindge
news.text:
Two Democrats will try in Tuesday’s general election to unseat Republican incumbents in Cheshire County House District 18, which takes in Dublin, Jaffrey and Rindge.

Rep. Rita Mattson of Dublin, who describes herself as a retired blue-collar worker, is vying for her second term, while Rep. Jim Qualey of Rindge, who holds a doctorate in physics and had a career as an engineer, is seeking his fourth.

Neither responded to multiple requests for an interview.

They face Democrats Allen Davis, a retired college educator and nonprofits leader, and Rory Lovett Sherman, a machinist, both of Dublin.

Property taxes

In interviews this week, Davis and Sherman talk about the need to reduce high property taxes and improve public services by reversing years of Republican-led cuts to taxes on businesses and investors.

“One of the reasons I’m running is that during the last 10 years when Republicans have controlled all levers of government, they have reduced taxes by as much as $1.5 billion on the wealthiest individuals and corporations and, therefore, the state keeps downshifting costs to the towns,” Davis said.

“So the towns then have the very unpleasant situation of do we want to have firefighters, do we want to have police officers, do we want to have the best schools possible, and if the answer is yes, the only answer is to raise property taxes, and that’s becoming unsustainable.”

He said he rejects the notion that cuts to taxes on businesses and on investors have a trickle-down effect and help people at all income levels.

Guns on campus

Meanwhile, Mattson and Qualey voted with the Republican majority in the N.H. House on a range of bills this year, including one to allow guns on college campuses.

That legislation stalled in the state Senate amid opposition from police officers, students and educators, including some from Keene State College.

On his campaign website, Qualey lists defending the 1st and 2nd Amendments as a priority.

“I believe in individual liberty and limited government interference in our lives,” he said on the website.

Another listed priority is opposing any new state income or sales tax. Lawmakers of both parties widely oppose this.

“Government should live within its means, not reach deeper into your pocket,” he said.

Another priority is to “support parental rights in education and give families real choices in how their children are educated.”

On her website, Mattson calls herself “an average citizen who is tired of the elitist lead government that wants us average citizens to not be recognized as individuals, that are having our rights as US citizens whittled away, our Constitution disregarded, and our country overrun by those who disregard the law.”

Childhood vaccines

She also says she is “against mandates for unproven vaccines. This is a personal decision and is between you and your doctor. I will never support mandates.”

Mattson and Qualey voted last year voted in favor of a bill to limit childhood immunization requirements to diseases identified in statute.

The bill, which didn’t clear the Senate, would have removed the authority of the state to adopt rules requiring immunization for additional childhood diseases.

They also both voted in favor of a bill last year to open to families at all income levels New Hampshire’s Education Freedom Account program, which provides taxpayer dollars to help parents pay to send their children to religious, private and home schools.

This was a partisan issue, with many Democrats voting against expansion of the school voucher program, arguing that public dollars should support public, not private, schools.

New revenue streams

Sherman said the state needs to look for “new revenue streams,” including potentially legalizing marijuana for recreational use, that could be used to provide more state support for public education and decrease the burden on local property taxpayers.

He opposes a general election ballot question that would allow voters to cap local school district property tax levies. Republican lawmakers put the question on the ballot as a way to address high property taxes by reducing increases in school spending.

“Yes that might keep property taxes right where they are currently for a little bit longer but you still haven’t solved the problem that our schools are regularly facing cuts, they are regularly facing shortages, they can not hire the teachers that they need because they are not offering competitive salaries across the state to attract teachers to come into the state,” Sherman said.

Rindge tends to be one of the most conservative areas of Cheshire County. In the 2024 presidential election, Democrat Kamala Harris carried the county, but lost in Rindge, where voters favored Republican Donald Trump, 2,348 to 1,380.
news.summary: Two Democrats will try in Tuesday’s general election to unseat Republican incumbents in Cheshire County House District 18, which takes in Dublin, Jaffrey and Rindge.
news.author: Rick Green

news.title: Is Ken Paxton’s Senate Campaign in Texas the Bitter End of Trumpism?
news.text:
“How are you gonna fix Ken’s fuckups?”
Dragging on a cigarette, he pointed to the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate candidate’s alleged corruption, his reputed infidelity, and the case of a plea deal his office offered to a Waco man charged with sexually abusing a young boy. “Just because you have all this money, how are you gonna just do as you please and nobody’s gonna say nothing?” Tracey remains a fan of the state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott. “He’ll win, so I’m happy about that.” But Paxton? “Get him out of there.”
If Paxton has lost voters like Tracey, Republicans might be in trouble. Texas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and this seat could determine who will control Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. Yet the collapse in Trump’s approval across the country has put even red states like Texas in play for Democrats, creating a powerful undercurrent that Paxton’s opponent James Talarico has surfed to a narrow but steady lead in the polls. That’s turned Texas into a money pit: $500 million has been blown on advertising already, thanks in part to at least $168 million pumped into the state by Elon Musk, and it’s on track to be the most expensive Senate race in history.
It didn’t have to be this difficult. Since 2002, the seat has been occupied by Senator John Cornyn, who ran for re-election with the backing of the Republican establishment and a sizable war chest. But in the primary, the president backed Paxton, a scandal-plagued culture warrior who went above and beyond Trump’s loyalty tests while Cornyn drew suspicion that he was fair-weather MAGA. Now Trump has placed a risky bet. These midterms are a referendum on the president, but this race more than any other is a gauge of his movement: Can a candidate with many of Trump’s failings but little of his charisma careen into the United States Senate?
This is the final sprint of the Paxton campaign, a frenetic bus odyssey dubbed the “Come and Take It Tour.” (There’s a cannon printed on the side of the bus.) The voyage has swept through the border towns of McAllen and Laredo, up through exurbs like Selma, just outside San Antonio, on to Austin and Waco and Dallas, then out through hundreds of miles of High Plains to the West Texas towns of Amarillo and Lubbock, then down to Corpus Christi for a rally with Trump himself.
“A MAN WITHOUT FLAWS?”
The pastor’s reminder that “King David was a flawed man” was met with scattered applause. If the subtext of this homily wasn’t clear enough, a protester soon made it explicit. “Why were you in Dubai?” a young man yelled as Paxton took the stage. He was swiftly bounced by security to chants of “USA!” from the faithful.
The protester was referencing the latest chapter of the biblical Paxton oppo file. The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve 2024 partying in Dubai with Tracy Duhon, his rumored mistress, as well as two men who were then fugitives from U.S. justice, one of whom had donated to Paxton. This indiscretion joins a long list of scandals that supporters of Paxton are willing to overlook to back the candidate (and, perhaps more importantly, keep Texas red). On the tour, they often invoked faith to make their case.
House Republican Darrell Issa, who served as Chairman of the House Oversight Committee and worked with Paxton when he was a crusading state attorney general, stumped for the candidate on his swing from San Antonio to Georgetown. When I asked why he felt compelled to campaign for Paxton given the baggage, Issa echoed Pastor Mendez.
“Is President Trump a man without flaws? No. But neither was Andy Jackson, neither was Bill Clinton, neither was Abraham Lincoln,” the congressman said. “So you judge somebody in elected office based on the honor that they bring to the office, the energy they bring and the initiatives that they’re involved in, and that’s where [Paxton] excels. So am I going to say that this is somebody that, like our savior, was without sin? No. But I’m not somebody without sin, and neither are any of the voters.”
Some would argue Paxton’s sins are more exotic than those of your ordinary Texan. He was charged with two counts of felony securities fraud by Texas prosecutors and in 2024 reached a deal to avoid a trial that involved paying nearly $300,000 in restitution. Separately, the Texas House impeached him in 2023 on charges of bribery, corruption and abusing his office. (Paxton has denied the allegations that led to his impeachment.) With state legislators under intense pressure from Trump, he was acquitted by the Senate. “Yes, it is true that my intervention through TRUTH SOCIAL saved Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from going down,” Trump boasted afterwards.
There’s also Paxton’s reputation for jet-setting: In his 11 years as attorney general, an Associated Press investigation found, Paxton spent an extraordinary amount of time traveling to plush locales including “California wine country, Caribbean resorts and European tourism hot spots.” It cost the taxpayers at least $1.9 million to cover the expenses of his security detail. And of course, there was the 2013 surveillance video that caught Paxton pocketing a man’s $1,000 Montblanc pen. (His campaign called the incident a “mix-up,” and Paxton returned the pen after he was contacted by a sheriff’s deputy.)
Even some of the ads supporting him carry a bit of a shrug. Angela Paxton, who is suing her husband for divorce on “biblical grounds,” which is King James for cheating, appears in a spot urging Texans to vote Republican down the ticket. “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room,” she says at the start of the ad, which ends without any further mention of the elephant.
For many in the Republican establishment, these indiscretions have pushed Paxton beyond the pale, but that’s little concern to the nominee’s supporters. “He may not have his life together,” said Janet, a Paxton backer from Corpus Christi, “but he’s better than the alternative.”
Kevin, a 62-year-old from the San Antonio suburbs, brought his wife to see Paxton speak in Selma. “I believe in this country there is a battle between good and evil,” he said. “I try to judge characters in a biblical sense.” Where does that leave Paxton, a man accused of violating quite a few of the Commandments? “I’m okay with Ken Paxton,” Kevin said, waving a hand as I ran down the list of transgressions. “I believe Trump is the best president we’ve ever had. And we got to have people in there to support him.”
Jason Norton, 50, a bearded and tattooed pastor of King’s Trail Cowboy Church who delivered the prayer at Paxton’s stop north of Dallas, had a similarly permissive view of his alleged infidelity. “Christian does not mean perfect. Nobody would approve of that. And I’m sure he probably regrets it. But what he did hurt himself and his family. What Talarico’s doing will hurt the entire state.”
In a quaint historic town north of Fort Worth, I met Steve Bannon at the Texas headquarters of his War Room podcast. A longtime Paxton backer, Bannon has spent much of this campaign season in the state, broadcasting to the Trump base while helping to advise the Republican’s campaign. “We have not seen the data yet that shows part of our coalition actually coming out and voting against Trump,” Bannon told me. “I think most of them are staying home. That’s a huge win for us. If they come out and vote against us, we’re fucked.”
“IT IS DEMONIC”
It doesn’t help the Democrat that, like many in the party, he dabbled in the kind of heady progressive rhetoric trendy in the early 2020s that’s anathema to red state voters. Among the hits, of which Texans are regularly reminded in Paxton’s speeches, Trump’s posts, and endless campaign ads: Talarico’s remark in 2021 that “God is nonbinary.” His comment in the same year that there are “six really common biological sexes” and referring to himself as “a Christian who hates Christianity.” His 2022 run for re-election to the Texas House, which he said would be a vegan campaign, reasoning that reducing meat consumption was “necessary to fight climate change.” His comment that the American flag is a “complicated symbol.”
Talarico has since walked some of these lines back, calling them “cringey” and “provocative.” But Musk’s money cannon ensures Texas voters are relentlessly confronted by them, and the race appears to have tightened in the final stretch of the campaign. For voters susceptible to these kinds of criticisms of Talarico, a Paxton rally provides a potent narrative. The notes from his stump speech that draw the loudest applause can drive the neutral observer to mild psychosis. We’re going to stop Sharia law from coming to Texas, goes one. The Pfizer vaccine was less than 1 percent effective, offers another. And of course: James Talarico wants to trans your kids.
That last bit is one of Paxton’s favorites, and it hit hard in some of the more incandescent-red counties we passed through. “I mean, this guy is really obsessed with transitions,” Paxton muses into the mic, winding up for the big delivery. “He wants to transition our kids, he wants to transition Texas off of the oil and gas industry.” (Wry pause.) “How about we transition him and his crazy ideas right out of Texas!” (Applause, cheers, hoots and hollers as Paxton steps back from the podium and smirks, almost bashfully, eyes darting back and forth as he soaks up the response.)
Some of the attacks on Talarico are more extreme. Paxton and a number of his campaign surrogates warned the Democrat would help usher Sharia law into Texas. When I met with Bannon, he introduced me to Glenn Story, a co-founder of Patriot Mobile, who’s active in Texas politics and counts Paxton as a friend. “I’m the one who told him to start talking about Sharia law,” Story said. “You go up to the Costco near me? Towelheads everywhere,” he said, using a slur for Muslims. “Come with me, I’ll show you.” Reluctant to spend my afternoon driving around looking for people who might appear Muslim, I declined.
At a stop in Sanger, a small town in a ruby red county north of Dallas, the star of the warm-up acts was Brandon Gill, a young House Republican who has emerged as a favorite among the party’s hard-line base. He walked out to a roaring welcome, and one man shouted “Brandon for President!” The heckle was deftly parried by Gill: “Let’s say Ken Paxton for Senate first.” As Gill ran through the list of well-worn criticisms of Talarico’s liberalism, Stacey, a woman in the crowd, shouted: “It’s demonic!”
“That’s right,” Gill replied. “It is demonic.”
Outside the venue, I spoke with Stacey and her friend Claire, two Paxton super-fans from nearby who called themselves “MAHA moms.”
“He seems like a nice man,” Stacey said of Talarico. “He’s just misguided. If he was my neighbor I’d vote for him to be on my HOA board. But not for the Senate.” They were confident that Paxton would keep the seat red. But Claire was concerned that her parents, both Republicans, had written in names in protest of Paxton’s candidacy.
BARE-KNUCKLE RADICALS
By this point I had seen Paxton deliver his stump speech, a 15-minute case for his Senate candidacy, some half a dozen times. At Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille, his delivery was pained. He seemed tired. He stumbled over his jokes, stopping and returning to the top after realizing he forgot the punchline. He struggled through a section meant to serve as a blistering indictment of his opponent, and he eventually spent several minutes looking down at the podium and listing Talarico’s crimes against Texas off a piece of paper as the crowd sat in silence.
At one point, an elderly man with a walker had had enough.
“More enthusiasm!” he shouted from the audience.
Paxton looked up from his papers and out into the crowd. “What?”
“More enthusiasm!” the man shouted again.
“Yes,” Paxton said meekly. “We all need a little more enthusiasm to go to the polls.”
Trump never hesitates to remind voters at his rallies that Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” The candidate has a lazy eye, a casualty of a childhood accident in which a berry was thrown at his face, requiring multiple surgeries, and a subsequent college basketball injury. He presents as meek, almost sheepish, and speaks in a monotone that belies his reputation as a bare-knuckle radical. He slurs his words and stumbles over his lines.
“Darrell,” he said at one stop, addressing Issa, “California arreddy has tt—you already have two senators, you d—we don’t need a third.” He’s less the guy you want to get a beer with, per the old campaign cliché, and more the guy you feel a bit sorry for when it’s his turn to address the room at a regional sales conference. At a Trump rally for Paxton in Lubbock, the president told the crowd that his praise of Jon Husted’s “very powerful ass” boosted the Senator’s election campaign in Ohio. “Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton,” he mused, “but I’m not sure your body is going to qualify.”
For Talarico and the Texas Democrats, who haven’t won a seat in the United States Senate since 1988, the Paxton campaign presents an extraordinary opportunity. “Billy Begala says: For the last 30 years, all you had to do to win in Texas is win the Republican primary and then go on vacation,” says veteran Democratic strategist Paul Begala, whose son Billy works in Texas politics. Paxton may have taken that truism a little too far. After announcing his candidacy for the Republican nomination in an appearance on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show, he “cleared his calendar and booked a hotel in Augusta, Georgia, during the storied Masters golf tournament,” according to the Associated Press, “a trip that cost Texas taxpayers at least $25,000.” Over July 4th weekend, while Talarico hit the trail, Paxton was in Europe, sightseeing in London and Iceland with his rumored mistress. As Talarico raised tens of millions of dollars from small-dollar donations throughout the summer, Paxton struggled to keep up. A week before the general election, Talarico had raised $158 million to Paxton’s $39 million.
“Ken is a different type of candidate in modern times,” Bannon said. “He has a hardcore grassroots base. But he’s not a good fundraiser.” In the primary against Cornyn, Paxton “didn’t raise any serious money. This was primarily a grassroots driven thing.”
Paxton, Bannon added, is “a populist fire breather who is not particularly charismatic.”
“PAXTON IS IN DEEP SHIT”
At the first of Trump’s appearances, in Corpus Christi, I watched from the press pen as Border Patrol union chief Paul Perez revved up the crowd with a question. “Is Texas Trump country?” he bellowed. A sea of bright red hats, bobbing in chaotic unison in a portside hangar, went ballistic. They had braved the rain and the dour mood spreading across the country to see a president they very much still believe in. But across Texas, the cracks in Trump’s support are deepening. Just two years after he beat Kamala Harris in the state by more than 1.5 million votes, The Economist’s poll tracker finds Trump’s approval in Texas is underwater by 18 points. This has fueled fears among the state’s Republicans that many of those who broke for Trump in 2024 could stay home this year or, God forbid, vote for the Democrat who thinks God is nonbinary.
“Clearly it has been a challenge for Ken to run during difficult personal times, but one of the reasons we admire him is that he is resilient,” said Matt Schlapp, the chairman of the Conservative Political Action Conference who held a fundraiser for Paxton at his Virginia home last month. “He will win this race but like last time there will be some fear and trembling along the way.”
Others in the coalition aren’t so sure. “Paxton is in deep shit,” Rich Baris, a pro-Trump pollster, said in a podcast appearance this week.
Trump may rally the base, but it’s hard to see how a historically unpopular president making the race about him helps with the broader electorate. After the president commanded Republicans to host a “Trumpapalooza” midterms convention that served more as a celebration of his presidency than a typical party congress, Paxton privately told donors the event hurt his campaign. “When we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said, according to audio of his comments obtained by The New York Times. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”
At the rally in Corpus Christi, Trump spoke for more than an hour. He extolled the glories of his presidency and made little mention of Paxton. After airing a supercut video of Talarico’s cringiest comments, Trump turned to the crowd. “The only man standing between Texas and this raging lunatic is a man named President Donald J. Trump, thank you!” he said. As the crowd went wild, Trump added: “And I need the help of Paxton.”
On the “Come and Take It” bus tour, Paxton was less a glimpse of Trumpism’s future than a showcase of what might be left behind when Trump is gone. The familiar accommodations were still required: overlook the scandals, forgive the personal failings, keep faith with the fighter standing between you and the forces of darkness. But there was none of the showmanship that made those demands easier to accept in Trump. The Paxton cocktail is the controversy without the charisma—and a test of whether a record of pure allegiance to Trump is enough for a Republican to win Texas. Defeat may well announce the bitter end of pure Trumpism, or at least prove that Trump alone is the movement. When he leaves the White House in 2029, what will remain of it?
news.summary: With allegations of corruption and a shortage of charisma, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas represents a fresh test for President Trump: Can his endorsement drag a flawed candidate to victory? Or will Trump’s own unpopularity take its toll?
news.author: Aidan McLaughlin,Mark Peterson

news.title: Kamala Harris Just Pulled Another Kamala Harris, This Time in Georgia
news.text:
Kamala Harris is still out rallying voters ahead of the midterm elections, and even two years later, she appears unable to shake the awkward persona that defined her 2024 presidential campaign. 

Late last week, the former vice president was dispatched to Mississippi to rally support for Democrat Scott Colom’s bid to flip the state’s Republican Senate seat. That appearance did not go particularly well. But Harris got yet another chance to redeem herself on Thursday, this time in Georgia, campaigning for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is rumored to have presidential ambitions of his own in 2028. 

Instead, she stumbled right out of the gate, managing to butcher the Georgia Democrat’s introduction.

“Let’s hear it for Jon Ossoff,” Harris said. “The next — and continuing senator from the state of Georgia.”

And if that weren’t bad enough, Harris also appeared to debut yet another accent along the way.

"Election time is a time to let them know we're too busy watching what you're doing to listen to what you're saying," Harris said. "You know what I'm saying."

news.title: UNDERCOVER VIDEO: Elissa Slotkin Lays Out Lawfare Plans If Dems Win Majority
news.text:
Michigan senator gushes to a total stranger about "every committee" in on the act.

Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin will apparently talk to anyone about the Democrats’ lawfare plans if they capture the majority in the House or Senate next week; all you have to do is ask.

Slotkin, while campaigning Thursday for congressional candidate Sean McCann, dished on what she has up her sleeve, according to an undercover video obtained exclusively by Townhall.

“I’m worried that we’re going to be too nice,” the person said to Slotkin in the video, triggering a smirk from the senator.

“What are we going to do to hold the Trump regime and its collaborators responsible? I’m talking prosecutions,” the person continued.

“I’m with you,” Slotkin responded. “So basically, assuming we win both houses, even if we just win one, we’ll come up– we have a list of, like, the ‘signature cases.’ So the things where it’s, like, so egregious, such a violation of law, such a corruption case, like– and we will have, in every committee, there will be the ‘signature cases’ that we– where we hold people accountable.”

Slotkin continued, “I just went to Hungary. I went over to Budapest in Hungary because they just got rid of their authoritarian leader after 16 years.” The Michigan senator said she was there seeking advice for how to go after the Trump administration.

“And I’m like, how did you handle 16 years of corruption? We don’t have that much, but we have so much,” she said. “And they did this ‘signature cases’ (strategy),” Slotkin said.

She went on to say “they’re the ones that people identify with,” specifically naming the ballroom project in the East Wing of the White House, the reflecting pool renovation on the Mall, “or $200 million in, you know, from the Defense Department.”

Slotkin then predicted — or warned — “So that’s what you’ll see basically in January.”

The Michigan senator is very possibly going to attempt to parlay that into a presidential campaign. Slotkin got elected by campaigning as a moderate, consensus builder. She featured Presidents Donald Trump and George W. Bush — for whom she worked — in campaign ads.

She has since been on a tear against Trump, blaming him for everything, and coming up with conspiracy theories about what he might do, including manufacturing a “national security incident” to change the outcome of the election.

Slotkin has been maneuvering for a potential run for president herself, including recently criticizing former Vice President Kamala Harris.

“If Democrats need new faces and new ideas, is that compatible with a presidential candidate who’s already lost?” Vox’s Astead Herndon asked Slotkin at the University of Chicago.

“No,” Slotkin said.

“Look, it’s a free country, so if she decides to run, that is her choice, okay?” she said. “I think you’re seeing stuff in the press, right? The fact that there are these articles talking about, like, should she, shouldn’t she, and there’s leaks about this and that, is part of this conversation about, like, she shouldn’t get in, maybe she should.”

“You know, it’s happening whether, you know, you see it above the surface or not,” Slotkin said. “But I just will be frank that I think the sentiment I’m describing is so strong of wanting new faces and big and bold ideas. It’s so universal. I think the public is going to meter out, and, like, I believe it so strongly that even if some of those more traditional folks you’ve heard of get in, it just won’t work.”

news.title: Texas Early Voting Nears 6M in Tight Talarico-Paxton Senate Race
news.text: More than 6.3 million Texans had voted early heading into Friday, the last day of early voting, in a Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton that polls still show as a toss-up. That figure, as of Wednesday, is a 50 percent increase from the 4.2 million Texans who had voted at the same point in 2022, according to a Newsweek analysis of voting data. Nationwide, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or by mail, nearly 10 million more than four years ago. Democrats are chasing their first statewide win in Texas since 1994, while Republicans, who hold a 53-47 Senate majority, are counting on a late push from their own voters, who tend to wait, to offset heavy early turnout in the state's big Democratic-leaning counties. Newsweek reached out to the Talarico and Paxton campaigns for comment via email on Friday. Early Voting Turnout in Texas In Harris County, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022, according to voting records reviewed by Newsweek. The county set a midterm record on the first day of early voting, when more than 127,000 people cast ballots, while Dallas County logged more than 88,000, its most on an opening day for any election, The Texas Tribune reported. Harris County has voted Democratic in recent elections by varying margins. In 2024, former Vice President Kamala Harris carried it by nearly 6 percentage points over Trump, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred won it by roughly 11 points over Republican Senator Ted Cruz. Turnout in Tarrant and Denton counties hit about 32 percent of registered voters by early this week. The Rio Grande Valley was running about 64 percent ahead of its 2022 pace, though all four counties there trailed the state average, and Starr and Willacy sat near 17 percent. Texas also has a record 19 million registered voters, 7.7 percent more than before the last midterm. The Secretary of State's office is expected to post Friday's totals over the weekend. How It Compares to Past Elections Democrats keep measuring this year against 2018, when Beto O'Rourke came within 2.6 points of Republican Senator Ted Cruz on the back of unusually high midterm turnout. About 53 percent of registered Texans voted that year, and nearly three-quarters of ballots were cast early or by mail. Against the last midterm, 2026 is well ahead. By the 10th day of early voting, 31.4 percent of registered voters had cast ballots in person, compared with 22.36 percent on the matching day in 2022, according to state data. The gap was there from the start: 4.12 percent on day one this year, 2.7 percent four years ago. A presidential year is another story. In 2024, in-person turnout had reached 38.87 percent by day 10. The race against 2018 has been tighter. After seven days, 23.4 percent of registered voters had voted, slightly behind the 24.3 percent at that point in 2018, a Texas Tribune analysis found. By early this week KERA had 2026 at about 26 percent, ahead of the roughly 24 percent recorded at the same stage eight years ago. Texas political analysts and experts have projected that as many as 10 million Texans could vote, near the 2018 rate. Who is voting has shifted as well. Through the first week, voters with a history in Democratic primaries made up 35 percent of early ballots, edging out the 33 percent with Republican primary history. Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist in Texas, who has watched the trend since March, when Democratic primary turnout beat Republicans' in raw numbers, says he is worried. "That was a concerning data point back then and it still worries me a bit now," he told Newsweek. Hispanic voters accounted for 18 percent of early voters through last Sunday, a point higher than in 2024 and 2 points above 2022, his data showed. Texas does not register voters by party, though, and primary history only goes so far. Democrats have tried to keep expectations in check. "It's fair to be skeptical, and even Texans, we are not counting any chickens here," Matt Angle, a Democratic strategist and director of the Lone Star Project, told Newsweek. James Talarico Vs. Ken Paxton: What Latest Polls Show Most recent surveys give Talarico a small edge. Almost none falls outside the margin of error. CNN released a poll on Thursday showing Talarico narrowly ahead with five days to go. ActiVote's newest survey of 400 likely voters, fielded October 22 to 28, had him up 52.1 percent to 47.9 percent, a lead that grew from 2 points a week earlier. Its margin of error was plus or minus 4.9 points. Texas Public Opinion Research had Talarico ahead 51 percent to 47 percent among 969 likely voters surveyed October 15 to 18, with a 3.9-point margin of error. His lead in that series has slipped by about a point a month since August, though he still carried independents 66 percent to 28 percent. A Fox News poll of 1,398 likely voters, taken October 15 to 19, found the race tied at 49 percent after Talarico led by 2 in September. Texas Southern University put the Democrat up 49 percent to 47 percent. Fox's September survey also caught how differently voters see the two men. Talarico's favorability was 8 points positive; Paxton was 18 points underwater. The University of Houston's Hobby School of Public Affairs had Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent among 2,000 likely voters polled October 10 to 14, with Libertarian Ted Brown at 3 percent and a 2.9-point margin of error. Party loyalty drove much of that result. Ninety-eight percent of Democrats in the poll backed Talarico, while 88 percent of Republicans backed Paxton and 6 percent planned to cross over. Mark Jones, a Rice University political scientist who co-authored the survey, told Houston Public Media those defections are "the difference between Paxton being ahead by a few points and Talarico being ahead by a few points." Why Republicans Are Banking on Election Day Republican voters in Texas are more likely than Democrats to wait for Election Day. Surveys by Joshua Blank, a political scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, show about two-thirds of Texas Democrats prefer to vote early, while Republicans are closer to evenly split. In Texas Politics Project polling, 40 percent of Republicans said they planned to vote on Election Day. The Democratic edge among voters with a primary history has been shrinking. CBS Texas reported it was down to nearly 57,000 ballots through Wednesday, and Republican researchers cited by NBC DFW said more than 1 million reliably Republican voters still had not voted as of Thursday. Mike Madrid, a former GOP strategist who has followed the race closely, said earlier this month that GOP turnout was the number he was watching most. "What I'm really keeping an eye on is what the turnout rate for Republicans is going to be," he told Newsweek. In his view, Democrats need what he called "the perfect trifecta" to win Texas: "very high Democratic turnout, a historic break of independents away from Republicans and depressed and defected turnout amongst Republicans. You need all three of those to win Texas." Turnout has lagged in rural counties. Republican consultant and data analyst Derek Ryan said on social media that turnout there was about 21 percent of registered voters, trailing the state's more heavily Democratic population centers. Rural margins alone may not be enough for Paxton. "Now he's going to crush Talarico in the rural areas, but that's not a large enough share," Jones told Newsweek. Governor Greg Abbott and Paxton spent Monday working deep-red territory, including a joint rally in Wichita Falls. Vice President JD Vance followed on Thursday in Parker County, west of Fort Worth, and told supporters to vote Friday or on Election Day. In Corpus Christi, Republican Greg Graves told KEDT he backed Senator John Cornyn in the primary but was fine voting for Paxton now. Steinhauser acknowledged that Democrats are more enthusiastic this year but did not count his party out. "I think that Republicans still can win," he said. "I still think there's a decent chance for them to win." Talarico vs. Paxton: An Expensive Senate Race Talarico holds a wide fundraising lead. He had raised $146.3 million in total campaign receipts through October 14, compared with $22.3 million for Paxton, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Outside money has narrowed the gap on the airwaves. Republican-aligned PACs backed by Trump, Senate Republican leaders and Elon Musk have committed more than $214 million to advertising supporting Paxton and attacking Talarico, according to media-tracking firm AdImpact. Talarico has also signed up more donors in Republican territory. A Newsweek analysis of third-quarter FEC filings found that Collin County, north of Dallas, gave Talarico $480,000 from about 1,850 donors and Paxton $223,000 from about 490. In Montgomery County, the GOP stronghold north of Houston that includes The Woodlands, Talarico raised $220,000 to Paxton's $162,000. The pattern held in West Texas. Talarico raised $96,086 from 306 Lubbock County donors in the third quarter, compared with $53,204 from 97 donors for Paxton, according to Newsweek's review of FEC records. Why Texas Senate Race Matters in 2026 Midterm Elections The race could help decide who controls the Senate. Republicans hold 53 seats, and Democrats need a net gain of four to take the majority. The seat opened when Paxton, the state's attorney general, beat Cornyn in the May runoff with 63 percent of the vote. President Donald Trump, who had called both men friends, endorsed Paxton on May 19. Talarico, a state representative from the Austin area, won the Democratic nomination in March over Representative Jasmine Crockett of Dallas. He has built his campaign around the cost of living, and voters have picked him over Paxton on that issue in every Texas Public Opinion Research poll since May. Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the race as Republicans defend a state Democrats have not won statewide in more than three decades. Trump visited Texas earlier this week, his third trip to the state in a month. Polls open at 7 a.m. on Tuesday and close at 7 p.m. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Kate Nalepinski and Trevor Davies
news.summary: That is a 50 percent increase from the 4.2 million Texans who had voted by the same point in the 2022 midterms.
