news.title: Edwardsville Nurse Jennifer Todd Takes On Rep. Mary Miller in Deep-Red Illinois District
news.text:
A nurse from Edwardsville with no prior political experience is mounting a challenge against U.S. Rep. Mary Miller in Illinois' 15th Congressional District, where Miller faced write-in candidate William Bonnett in the 2024 general election. Democrat Jennifer Todd says her years treating patients who struggled to afford care pushed her into the race, and she's built her campaign around affordability, farming and health care in a district Miller carried by 42 points in her last contested race.

Todd, a lifelong Metro East resident, emerged from a four-way Democratic primary in March with 45.8% of the vote, according to St. Louis Public Radio. She lives less than a mile outside the district's boundaries in Edwardsville and has said she plans to move to Logan County if she wins in November. The 15th District wraps around the more Democratic-leaning 13th District, stretching from East St. Louis through Springfield to Champaign-Urbana, and the Cook Political Report rates it solidly Republican.

A District Built for Republicans

The numbers explain why Miller has coasted in past elections. In 2022, Republican Darren Bailey beat Gov. JB Pritzker 69% to 28% in the district, and Donald Trump topped Kamala Harris there by 69% to 29% in 2024, per the same St. Louis Public Radio report. Miller herself dispatched Democratic challenger Paul Lange 71.1% to 28.9% in 2022 and beat Erika Weaver with 73.4% of the vote in 2020, according to The Telegraph. She won a third term in 2024 against a write-in candidate, and the district itself covers most of Central Illinois, stretching from the Mississippi River to the Indiana border across all or part of 35 counties.

Miller, a third-generation cattle and grain farmer, serves on the House Agriculture, Education and Labor committees and belongs to the House Freedom Caucus. She has backed President Trump's agenda on most issues, supports his efforts to increase arrests and deportations of people without legal status, and backs his campaign against what he calls gender ideology in schools. She has also denounced the commission to investigate the January 6 insurrection. Miller points to bipartisan rural broadband and crop insurance legislation as among her legislative successes, and she voted to fund crop insurance while also voting to cut water runoff regulations for farmers and ranchers.

Fundraising Gap and a Quiet Campaign

Miller holds a commanding financial edge heading into the general election, entering the period with $833,235.60 in cash on hand against $34,505.79 in campaign debt, according to The Telegraph. Todd's campaign reported $54,330.57 in contributions, $35,640.03 in operating expenses and just $9,223.94 in cash on hand. Despite the imbalance, Miller has run what Politico's Illinois Playbook described as a light campaign footprint this year, and she did not respond to repeated interview requests about her race against Todd. She also did not respond to survey questions posed by the State Journal-Register.

Politico reported that Miller submitted six Community Project Funding requests for fiscal year 2026 after not submitting any from fiscal years 2021 through 2025, a shift that comes amid concerns among Illinois farmers about prices, tariffs and fertilizer. Todd's supporters argue that a combination of Democratic turnout and soft Republican enthusiasm could make the race closer than polling trends would suggest, though the district's lean remains steep.

Medicaid and Rural Hospitals Take Center Stage

Health care sits at the heart of Todd's pitch. She says constituents are bracing for Medicaid work requirements slated to begin next year. The enacted reconciliation package is expected to leave roughly 10 million more people uninsured and cut an estimated $911 billion in federal Medicaid spending. Todd supports preserving Medicaid to help keep rural hospitals open, saying facilities in the district rely on the program to pay bills and retain staff, and she has said Medicaid visit numbers for physical, speech and occupational therapy are being cut.

The stakes for rural providers are significant. KFF has reported that nearly half of rural-hospital births and one-fifth of inpatient discharges nationwide are funded by Medicaid, which covers one in four rural adults — a higher share than in urban areas. KFF estimates the enacted reconciliation package could shrink federal Medicaid spending in rural areas by $137 billion over 10 years, pressure that the organization says could lead to staff layoffs, fewer services or further hospital closures.

Farm Bill Fight and Foreign Policy

Agriculture remains the leading industry in the district, and Todd has made the stalled federal farm bill a central line of attack. She said she would have voted against the farm bill the House passed earlier this year, arguing it does nothing for family farms and criticizing cuts to SNAP and agricultural research programs she says are hurting local farmers. She's also flagged rising diesel costs as a vulnerability for farmers who depend on fuel to run equipment, warning that higher overhead translates into higher grocery prices for everyone.

Todd has tied foreign policy to pocketbook concerns as well, saying the war in Iran has added unnecessary costs for farmers already strained by the stalled farm bill. She said she would vote to rein in Trump's military action in Iran and the administration's sweeping tariffs, and she has called for greater congressional oversight of military spending. On immigration, Todd says she supports strong border protections alongside dignity for families of incarcerated and deported people, and she wants more federal immigration staff and additional attorneys and judges to clear backlogs facing people seeking green cards and citizenship.

Early voting is already underway in the district, with Election Day set for Tuesday, Nov. 3. Whether Todd's focus on affordability and health care can make a dent in one of the most Republican districts in the country remains to be seen, but Miller has faced opponents in recent cycles, including Democrats in 2020 and 2022 and a write-in candidate in 2024.
news.summary: Edwardsville nurse Jennifer Todd faces Rep. Mary Miller in Illinois' 15th District, her first contested race in this heavily Republican seat since 2022.

news.title: If the Polls Turn Out to Be Wrong, This Will Be the Reason Why
news.text:
There are a lot of reasons to be skeptical of polling this year, and a new Washington Post survey out of Kansas just exposed one of the biggest.

Frankly, the polls have been very suspect throughout the Trump era. The most infamous miss belongs to Ann Seltzer, whose final 2024 Iowa poll had Kamala Harris ahead by three points. Trump carried the state by 13, which put the forecast off by a staggering 16 points. That poll destroyed her reputation and forced her into retirement.

I've been hesitant to jump on the bandwagon that the polls are deliberately skewed to suppress GOP turnout. Polling is an imperfect science, and I don't want to wave away every number simply because it looks good for Democrats. But it’s also undeniable that factors this cycle may be throwing the polls way off, and the Post just documented one of them as it happened.

The Post partnered with George Mason University's Schar School to survey the Senate race between Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Democrat challenger Adam Hamilton, one of the least-polled competitive Senate contests in the country. Scott Clement, the Post's polling director, explained what the team ran into once the calls went out.

After more than 85,000 phone calls and nearly 50,000 text messages, a potential problem emerged.Democrats were far more enthusiastic about taking the poll than Republicans were. Registered Democrats were more than twice as likely as registered Republicans to complete the survey after answering an interviewer’s call — 32 percent versus 12 percent — with a similar partisan gap when texting voters to complete the survey online.

"This was a supersize version of a concern that has vexed pollsters for the last decade," Clement wrote.

ICYMI: There's a Spicy New Plot Twist in the Ilhan Omar Sham Marriage Scandal

Mark Rozell, dean of George Mason's Schar School of Policy and Government, had his own theory about why Republicans stayed silent.

"The partisan enthusiasm gap likely explains the disconnect between Democratic and Republican willingness to respond… With an unpopular president, inflation, a war that Trump voters never asked for, the lack of GOP enthusiasm is not surprising," Rozell said.

He went further, wondering aloud about the mood on the right. "Are Republican voters this late in the election cycle feeling so down about their party's chances that they just don't want to talk about it?" Rozell asked.

That's one way to read it. I read it very differently.

We’ve seen polls underestimate the support of Trump and Republicans before, even at the height of MAGA enthusiasm. We know how leftists let politics dictate every aspect of their lives, while Republicans tend to care more about living their lives than going out and spending hours a day protesting — or taking time away from things that matter to respond to a poll.

Republicans who hang up on a pollster aren't necessarily demoralized. They may simply have more important things to do, or perhaps they're distrustful of the pollster. And it’s not like they have no reason to be.

The pollsters have chased down thousands of additional Republican voters to balance the sample. Clement admitted even that may not have been enough. "It's possible those efforts fell short," he added.

This pattern goes well beyond Kansas. As PJ Media previously reported, CNN anchor Boris Sanchez asked pollster Frank Luntz last week whether surveys under-sample the less-engaged voters Trump tends to turn out. Luntz, who has warned Democrats against complacency heading into the midterms, didn't hesitate.

"We know that they don't respond to phone calls," Luntz told CNN. "We know that in the exit polling back in 2016, and I say this publicly because I want people to hear this — you know, I teach at West Point. I cannot lie, cheat, or steal. The cadets can't. I can't. — I got 2016 wrong. I believed in the exit polls. Trump voters walked away, refused to participate because they thought that it was against them."

I’m not going to tell you that the polls are all definitely wrong. Could they be? Sure. There’s plenty of reason to believe this year will feature another heaping pile of lousy polls that grossly underestimated Republican support. If that’s the case, we’ll know the reason why.

news.title: MS NOW Cries ‘Election Cheating’ While Ignoring Democrats’ History
news.text:
MS NOW once again warned viewers about Trump’s efforts to manipulate elections. During Wednesday’s The Weeknight, the panel’s discussion of alleged Republican election “cheating” left out some significant history from the Democratic Party’s own redistricting battles.

Co-host Luke Russert claimed Republicans were moving toward “malfeasance” because they were “getting clobbered at the polls.”

Followed with a profanity-laced dismissal of President Donald Trump, co-host Michael Steele called out how Americans “cannot be disenchanted from the act that we are called upon by the Constitution in this moment to do,” “despite whatever hiccup or roadblock or BS Donald Trump wants to put in front of us…”

President of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee John Bisognano then joined the discussion to accuse Republicans of manipulating congressional districts, and declared “I think the through line on all of it is cheating, right?”

Bisognano proceeded to accuse Trump of launching a redistricting effort after signing the One Big Beautiful Bill, suggesting Republicans anticipated the legislation's economic consequences and wanted to manipulate electoral maps in response (Click “expand”):

And that's a scary thing to look back. They knew, they knew what they were doing to the economy then. They went back to a moment and said, “what we did is going to be really damaging and only going to get worse, so we better start cheating now.”And they did. He stood there and said, “we're going to redraw Texas and we're going to redraw more states.” And the only thing he didn't count on, to your point, was the American people fighting back. And luckily for us, you know, we had Attorney General Holder and leader Jeffries in the mix to make sure that we were fighting back as hard as we could. And we fought this back so that this redistricting gambit is going to have backfired. But I'll tell you right now, everyone needs to get out and vote, and they need to do it in mass and in every possible region and, and district and state needs to get out and vote. And that's what I've spent most of my career working on. I think it's the most important thing.

But Bisognano's criticism conveniently overlooked Democrats' own redistricting history, particularly in New York.

In February of 2022, Hochul signed a congressional map drawn by the Democrat-controlled Legislature that sought to improve her party's position in the state's congressional delegation, leaving Republicans with as few seats as possible. The map was challenged in court, and New York's Court of Appeals ultimately invalidated it in April of 2022. 

Democrats weren't finished, however. In February 2024, following the 2022 midterms, Hochul signed another Democrat-drawn congressional map ahead of the presidential election. The new boundaries gave Democrats a slight advantage in several competitive districts, and held the potential to improve their position in the battle for control of the House. 

While Bisognano was accusing Republicans of “cheating,” his own party had a recent history of pursuing partisan advantages through congressional redistricting, including an earlier attempt that was actually ruled unconstitutional.

The 2024 Iowa poll is another striking example of politicians' use of polling numbers to suggest an election is decided. The Des Moines Iowa Poll showed Kamala Harris leading Trump, yet Trump won the state by approximately 13 points (an almost 16 point polling error).

Polling errors were also found by The American Association for Public Opinion Research in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections. The 2016 poll contained errors to many battleground states, and suggested a totally different picture of the country. The 2020 polls overstated the Biden-Trump margin by an average of 3.9 percentage points nationally, and 4.3 points in state level polling.

There’s a reason Democratic campaigns tell supporters to not put trust in the polls, not to rest on their laurels, and to run through the tape. It’s basic political strategy: keep voters motivated, avoid complacency, and get out the vote. Encouraging turnout is not evidence for election cheating.

The circumstances surrounding the Trump administration's current election-related legal disputes are not identical to state-level redistricting, and each deserves examination on its own merits. But Democrats' record is certainly relevant when their representatives make sweeping accusations about the other party's motives.

If partisan redistricting is a threat to election fairness, that standard should apply regardless of which party benefits. Apparently, that was a piece of history The Weeknight panel wasn't particularly interested in discussing.

news.title: Scott Colom Is Challenging Democrats to Stop Writing Off Mississippi
news.text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom is fighting for more than just a Senate seat to represent Mississippi. His campaign has challenged the political assumptions that have kept Democrats from competing across the South and proving that Mississippi is not beyond reach. In an exclusive interview with The Root’s publisher Ashley Allison, Colom discussed why Democrats have struggled to secure enough votes in Mississippi and why he believes the state is more competitive than party leaders have allowed voters to imagine. Check out The Root’s full interview with Scott Colom here.

With just days until the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the stakes couldn’t be higher.

“The reason Democrats haven’t won in Mississippi is one, they haven’t been trying, and two, people don’t believe we can do it,” Colom told Allison.

Mississippi hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than 44 years. And a Black senator hasn’t represented the state since Reconstruction. That’s a political history Colom is determined to challenge.

RELATED: Mississippi Has Never Elected a Black U.S. Senator. Now, Scott Colom Could Change That

Despite the odds, his campaign has brought the once-unthinkable possibility of a Democratic victory into the conversation. Several polls have predicted a win for Trump-backed incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to the Clarion Ledger. But amid redistricting battles and economic concerns, Colom sees an opening to build a coalition that could defy expectations.

“Mississippi’s never been a lost cause,” Colom said, adding that the state has “been a betrayed cause.”

The numbers help explain his argument. In 2024, President Donald Trump secured 60% of the vote in Mississippi, while Sen. Roger Wicker won reelection by 26 points, according to NBC News. In 2020, Joe Biden received 41% of the vote compared with Trump’s 58%, numbers that largely echoed the results of the 2016 presidential election, too.

But Colom argues those results don’t tell the whole story. For years, Democrats have treated Mississippi as a political write-off rather than investing in the communities and voters who could make the state competitive. Voters, he said, deserve more than campaign-season lip service.

“When you don’t compete in a place like Mississippi, what you’re telling those voters is… You just don’t matter enough to us to actually fight for your vote and inspire you to actually get out there and do something about it,” Colom added.

It’s a message that carries particular weight for Black Mississippians, whose votes have been central to Democratic victories nationally but haven’t translated into statewide representation their numbers might suggest. Colom’s campaign is making the case that those voters deserve to be courted, heard and invested in.

For more than a year, Colom has been taking that message directly to communities across Mississippi, working to build the kind of grassroots support that conventional political wisdom has often dismissed.

“What I think we’re showing in this moment– and it’s not something I’m doing, it’s something the people of Mississippi are doing– is we’re showing that we actually matter,” he said. 

That people-powered approach has attracted national attention, including endorsements from former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama. But beyond that, Colom’s candidacy has put questions of representation, economic affordability and political accountability at the center of the high-profile race. A historic victory could also force Democrats to reconsider how they approach the South. 

“Creating a belief is something that one person can’t do. Only a group of people can do that. It takes city by city, county after county, community after community. And we did it the hard way,” he added. “Because we did it that way, we’re ready for this moment, and we’re ready to win.”

In an exclusive interview with The Root, the Democratic candidate explains why Mississippi shouldn't be written off and what it will take to change the state's political landscape.

news.title: Terrence Howard hints at potential presidential run in cryptic message and subtle swipe at Trump
news.text:
Terrence Howard has suggested he may well run to be president in the future, as he expressed his desire to sit down and chat with Donald Trump.

The US midterm elections take place next week, and while Donald Trump will still be president on November 4, his party may no longer have a grip on Congress.

While the American public are currently debating on who to vote for in the midterms, two years from now Americans will be going to the polls once more to vote on who they want to be the next president.

While President Trump is prohibited from running due to 22nd Amendment, Howard has suggested he could be a surprise inclusion on the ballot paper.

The Empire actor was asked if he was looking forward to voting in the midterms next week, which lead to him expressing bigger ambitions of running the country one day.

"Yes. I'm looking forward to becoming president," he told TMZ.

Seemingly taking a dig at the Trump administration, Howard added: "If they're not going to make a difference, somebody's got to do something."

Howard added to TMZ that he'd like to sit down with the current president to speak about the lasting impact of slavery, arguing descendants should not have to pay federal taxes for 400 years.

JD Vance and Marco Rubio are seen as the main favourites to be the Republican candidate in 2028, while much talk remains as to whether Kamala Harris will run again for the Democrats.

Trump has long stated he would like to run for a third term, despite the fact he's not allowed to do so.

Under the 22nd Amendment of the United States Constitution, no person can be elected to the office of the president more than twice.

It states: "No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice, and no person who has held the office of President, or acted as President, for more than two years of a term to which some other person was elected President shall be elected to the office of the President more than once."

The amendment adds: "But this Article shall not apply to any person holding the office of President when this Article was proposed by the Congress, and shall not prevent any person who may be holding the office of President, or acting as President, during the term within which this Article becomes operative from holding the office of President or acting as President during the remainder of such term."

However, earlier this year, Trump said he “would love to run” for a third term, but ultimately conceded that 'the law is very strong' when it comes to prohibiting it.

“The law is very strong on that,” Trump stated. “The 22nd Amendment is very clear, and I believe in following the law.”

news.title: Early voting jumps as millions more Americans vote ahead of midterms
news.text:
Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance and particularly sharp increases in states hosting competitive Senate races, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data five days before Election Day.

The surge is especially pronounced in Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor’s races. More than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50 per cent increase.

Advance voting has also increased more than 30 per cent from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races.

In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83 per cent.

The data, compiled by the AP, offers a glimpse of early voter participation five days before an election that will determine control of Congress and other key contests.

Across the country, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots, nearly 10 million more than in 2022. The figures cover 47 states and Washington, D.C., compared with 48 states and the nation’s capital four years ago.

In states that provide information on voters’ party affiliation, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans have cast ballots early. Those figures do not account for all early voters nationwide or indicate which candidates received their votes.

The increase comes as voters prepare to decide control of Congress two years into U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, with Republicans holding the House and the Senate.

Voters have turned out in droves during Texas’ two-week early in-person voting period, which ends Friday.

In Harris County, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022.

The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris defeated Trump by nearly six percentage points in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

This year, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched Senate race, while Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking reelection against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trump visited Texas earlier this week, his third trip to the state in a month.
news.summary: Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance of tightly contested races.

news.title: Trump escalates legal challenges against states as Election Day nears
news.text:
Donald Trump’s administration is intensifying legal action against US states with just days to go until a midterm election that will decide the balance of power in Washington during his final two years in office.

In Alaska, the Justice Department filed an amended lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block the certification of results in the event of a narrow Republican loss in a hugely consequential Senate race, citing a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a spoiler candidate to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.

In California, meanwhile, the DOJ is escalating its pressure campaign against state election officials, issuing subpoenas as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by non-citizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.

The moves, taken together, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state elections, which are administered locally under the US constitution. As November 3 nears, election officials around the country have told ⁠Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington.

The dispute in Alaska, home to one of about 10 highly competitive Senate races, could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority from Republicans.

If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they could launch probes into Trump’s administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war in Iran.

On Friday, Trump will campaign in Florida, hoping to galvanize his supporters in a state he won handily in 2024 but where early voting has tilted toward Democrats.

It will be his latest stop in a state Republicans usually expect to win, following campaign events earlier this week in Mississippi and South Carolina.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday.

“The last year and a half, it’s been difficult,” she told the crowd on Thursday at an event in Macon, Georgia. “Now we’re in the phase where we can do a whole lot.”

More than 44 million Americans had already voted as of Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, less that two million shy of the total from the 2022 midterms.

At a polling center on Thursday in Columbus, Ohio, home to highly competitive Senate and governor’s races, election official Antone White said turnout was about twice as high as 2022.

Among those waiting to cast their ballot was Sadirah Simmons, a senior citizen living on a fixed income. “The economy is not getting any better,” she said. “You have to go out and vote if you want change.”

ALASKA SENATE DISPUTE

In its revised lawsuit in Alaska on Thursday, the Justice Department wrote that operatives for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola orchestrated a “sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters.”

The New York Times reported Wednesday that the operatives recruited a candidate with the same name as incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy called for a state investigation and said in an interview with News Nation that any finding of illegality “may in fact impact whether someone is seated in the US Senate.”

Alaska election officials called the amended lawsuit “meritless” in a court filing on Thursday night, saying it has “cast a cloud over Alaska’s election that is contrary to the public interest.”

Peltola’s campaign did not immediately respond to the amended complaint but has previously said it had “no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races.

Daniel J. Sullivan has previously denied that his aim was to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.

“This guy’s existence is gonna hurt Mary Peltola so much more than it helps her,” said Alaska-based elections and campaign attorney Scott Kendall. But with so few undecided voters left, he added, the revelations were unlikely to impact the outcome of the race.

Julie Wyatt, a 62-year-old logistics manager who lives in the capital of Juneau, said such trickery was nothing new in Alaskan politics, and she still planned to vote for Peltola.

“If the Republicans are this desperate, Mary has them on the ropes,” she wrote in an email.

CALIFORNIA SUBPOENAS

In California, meanwhile, the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week as part of a DOJ probe into alleged non-citizen voting, according to copies of the documents seen by Reuters on Thursday.

“At every step, the US Department ​of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach,” Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement ​on Thursday. “Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”

A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the subpoenas but said that California and the federal government “agree that non-citizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law.”

news.title: AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Virginia on Election Day
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — In Virginia, two incumbent Republicans are fending off tough Democratic challengers in U.S. House races in a difficult midterm climate for the GOP. Voters will also decide whether to reelect their Democratic U.S. Senator to a fourth term and decide a ballot measure that would codify reproductive rights in the state constitution.

A Democratic win in either congressional race could push the party closer to regaining control of the chamber. Democrats need to win three more seats than in 2024 to claim the majority and see President Donald Trump’s plunging approval rating as an opportunity to score wins in competitive districts.

The 2nd Congressional District, which includes the city of Virginia Beach and the Virginia portion of the Delmarva Peninsula, has one of those competitive races. Rep. Jen Kiggans, the Republican incumbent, faces former Rep. Elaine Luria, a Democrat who lost the seat to Kiggans in 2022 after redistricting. Kiggans won that race by less than four percentage points.

The 2nd Congressional District has passed between Republicans and Democrats several times in the past few decades. In 2024, Kiggans defeated a different Democratic challenger by a margin of less than four percentage points. In the same election, Trump won the district over Kamala Harris by less than one-half of one percentage point. In the 2025 gubernatorial race, the area favored Democrat Abigail Spanberger.

Kiggans, a Navy veteran endorsed by Trump, has campaigned on her record in office and has attacked Luria for opposing a proposal to ban congressional stock trading in 2022, a position the latter reversed this year. Luria, also a Navy veteran, has highlighted her opponent’s support for Trump’s war in Iran, a resonant issue in a district with a significant military population.

Luria, who campaigned alongside Virginia U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, had raised about $8 million as of mid-October, according to financial disclosure documents. Kiggans, who campaigned with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., raised about $7.6 million.

In Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, Rep. Rob Wittman, a nine-term Republican, faces what may be his most difficult reelection battle yet against Democrat Shannon Taylor, a county prosecutor. The bellwether district in the eastern part of the state, which includes Jamestown, Williamsburg, Yorktown and some of Richmond’s suburbs, reelected Wittman by a margin of nearly 13 percentage points in 2024.

Wittman has asked voters to reelect him so he can continue being a voice for the district in Congress. Taylor has focused her campaign on rooting out corruption in Washington and painted Wittman as benefiting from a corrupt system.

news.title: Democrats see AI hate as winning issue heading into 2028
news.text:
Driving the news: 2028 contenders including Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Jon Ossoff and more have all increased their AI commentary in recent months, per new research from Upswing, conducted on behalf of Reset Tech, a nonprofit advocating for tech regulation. 

Among 21 Democrats named as potential 2028 contenders, tech mentions on X nearly quadrupled, and press release mentions nearly tripled since the start of the year.

Tech is now the second-most common topic in releases, trailing only jobs and the economy, with the highest concentration of mentions around data centers and phone bans in schools. To gather the data, Upswing analyzed nearly 30,000 X posts from 38 accounts associated with 21 potential presidential contenders and 3,868 press releases from 16 officeholders between Jan. 1 and Oct. 15. 

Between the lines: Democrats are galvanizing around AI as a winning issue. 

Democrats are "taking a meaningful advantage" on AI after the topic was initially seen as a "jump ball" for both major political parties, Rishi Bharwani, U.S. director of Reset Tech, told Axios. AI regulation has gone from the back burner to a top issue over the last six months, he added. While the economy is still what matters most to voters, AI is increasingly part of the financial conversation as it dominates markets and the macroeconomic backdrop. 

Zoom in: It's not just messaging. 

While data center bans have been proposed in Democratic- and Republican-majority states, New York is so far the only one to pass a moratorium.House Democrats drafted a resolution opposing government bailouts for AI companies if the so-called "bubble" bursts.There are also a variety of legislative proposals, including model transparency measures and kill switches. 

Zoom out: This comes amid a groundswell of anti-AI sentiment among voters.

Republicans are distancing themselves from Trump to varying degrees. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-Fla.), for example, has been among the loudest about state-level regulation on the technology. 

The bottom line: Democrats are coalescing around a more critical stance on AI, but whether it meaningfully impacts elections remains to be seen.

news.title: Why these Florida Republicans say they’re voting for Democrats
news.text:
Some Florida Republicans say they’re voting for Democrats this cycle, in large part, because they’re fed up with one-party rule — even though it’s their own party.

Palmetto Bay resident Tom Gray, 81, has only strayed from his Republican Party line three times over the last 50 years: once in 1976 to vote for Jimmy Carter, again in 2024 for Kamala Harris and now, in 2026, to vote for Democrats David Jolly and Angie Nixon.

While Gray opted for President Donald Trump during his first two runs, by 2024 he’d decided “anything is better than Trump.” Since then his rage against Trump has only grown.

Even though Trump’s not on the ballot this year, he’s treating Florida’s midterms as a referendum on the man in charge.

The individual Democratic candidates this cycle didn’t matter that much to him. Jolly, the former Republican congressman running for governor, and Nixon, the progressive community organizer and state representative campaigning for U.S. Senate, earned his vote because it’s “really just anger at the party, the Republican Party.”

That frustration is rooted, in part, in how he’s seen Trump’s mass deportation agenda affect his Miami community, and in concerns about the rising cost of living.

“They’ve overdone going after the people that are the heartbeat of South Florida. Throwing a lot of them away is pretty heartless,” Gray said. “I’m an old gringo, but what’s fair is fair and a lot of these people own homes, pay taxes and are getting kicked out of our country.”

He is among the white voters that make up the most loyal base and vast majority — 78% — of the Republican Party in Florida. He’s still voting for Republicans down-ballot.

But he’s also the kind of voter that could help deliver a statewide win for Democrats this year, after almost three decades of Republican control of the state. Democrats have a steep voter registration disadvantage in Florida, and for any chance of winning statewide next week, they need registered Republicans to either stay home or vote blue.

That means party switchers could be a decisive voting block in Tuesday’s statewide races.

Multiple recent statewide polls show Democrats have been more effective in pulling crossover votes this election cycle than Republicans.

Polls released this month by the University of North Florida, Stetson University and the James Madison Institute all found that Democrats Jolly and Nixon were both getting a larger share of Republican voters than their opponents were capturing of Democratic ones.

UNF found the largest differential, with 11% of registered Republicans planning to vote for Jolly and 5% of Democrats planning to vote for Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds.

Donalds, who would be Florida’s first Black governor if elected, has been making concerted efforts to convince Black Democrats to vote in his favor in recent weeks. He’s captured some high-profile support, and at least one poll, conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy, showed him receiving a significantly larger share of cross-party voters than Jolly.

But it remains unclear who will benefit more from the pivotal voters opting for candidates outside their party registration. St. Pete Polls recently found Donalds and Jolly receiving roughly the same share of voters registered with the opposing party.

Checks and balances

For the Republicans voting for Democratic candidates, much of the reasoning comes down to being fed up with one-party trifectas in both the state and federal governments.

Republican Manatee County Commissioner George Kruse has been an outspoken supporter of two Democrats: Jolly and Democratic congressional candidate Kelly Kirschner. For both of them, the argument he’s been making to his Republican friends is that the government simply works better when there’s friction and veto power at play.

“Trump is a mess and at some point, we need people up there in Congress who are actually gonna push back on this stuff,” he said.

On the state level, Kruse said, the argument is similar: “You have a supermajority in the House, a supermajority in the Senate, complete control in the Cabinet and Governor’s Mansion, effectively complete control of the judicial system, because virtually every judge has been appointed by a Republican at this point in time. There’s no checks and balance.”

Kruse said he’s not voting for Nixon because of her support for ending the filibuster — the requirement that the Senate reaches a 60-member consensus to pass legislation instead of a simple majority.

But other Republicans are.

In recent election cycles, Democrats have put forth centrist candidates like Jolly in hopes of bringing Republican crossover voters. Nixon, who’s built a groundswell of grassroots support on the left, has shown she’s also winning over some white Republicans.

Multiple polls show that, like Jolly, Nixon has been pulling more supporters from Florida’s majority party than Republican Sen. Ashley Moody has drawn crossover Democrats.

Jim Smith, 88, spent most of his life in Coconut Grove and retired in Fort Myers. The former chief financial officer has already cast a mail ballot this year, opting for multiple Democrats at the top of the ticket, also largely in protest of the president.

“My big problem right now is really all about Trump,” he said. “I can’t stand the guy.”

He’s hoping that giving Democrats a sliver of power will moderate his party. He wants to see fixes to Social Security and have the U.S. get out of its war with Iran.

“I think we need to move a little bit to the left,” he said of his support for Nixon. “I think we’re so far to the right.”

Neither Gray, Kruse nor Smith are interested in changing their lifelong voter affiliations — but they hope their wildcard protest votes send a clear message next week.

“I’m still a Republican, and I’m hoping that Republicans will come back to the way they should be,” Smith said. “But they’re just not there yet.”

news.title: On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote  - Guyana Inquirer – Daily Guyana
news.text:
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Leaning over plates of tamales, pan dulce, and sugar skulls, community organisers and local residents in the border city of Brownsville remembered the dead.

This year’s Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, vigil honoured victims of state violence, including those killed in immigration enforcement and detention. Just days before the US midterm election on November 3, the event reverberated in a region long subject to Washington, DC’s shifting political winds.

“The atmosphere here in the Rio Grande Valley when it comes to ICE detentions and the ICE raids, there’s just the overall feeling amongst folks that there’s no real due process to this,” said Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser.

“What is it that we can do to move together and build together to try to make it past this, and make that change that we seek?”

Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border and immigration policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia raised her hand to ask advice on how to find a lawyer able to navigate the aggressively shifting policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has used both an increase in physical enforcement, as well as a reinterpretation of administrative policies, to fuel its mass deportation campaign.

Garcia’s aunt, a well-known member of the community in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks ago, after being called to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) hearing. There she learned she had missed a court date related to her immigration status.

In the stress of the moment, she signed a voluntary deportation form.

“Within 36 hours, she was deported,” Garcia told Al Jazeera, tucked between bookshelves. “People are waking up, and they’re remembering that politics, regardless of what branch you’re in, it’s going to impact you every day.”

Shifting dynamics

Views on immigration are complex in the Rio Grande Valley, a geographic and cultural region located in subtropical southeast Texas with about 1.5 million residents. That complexity has only increased in recent years as border policy and immigration enforcement have become increasingly partisan, leading, reformers say, to dramatic policy swings that prevent more sustainable solutions.

It is not difficult to find Latino – or Tejano, the local term for Texans of Latino descent – residents wary of the years preceding Trump’s return to office. After the restrictive policies of Trump’s first term, border crossings increased dramatically under US President Joe Biden, fuelled in part by the end of a COVID-era policy that made asylum seekers wait for their cases to be processed in Mexico.

Some felt the border region was left to deal with the fallout from the influx. That discontent has been credited, in part, with Trump’s success in the once-reliably Democratic region in the 2024 presidential election.

In Hidalgo County, home to the city of McAllen, Trump won 51 percent of the vote in 2024, a three-point margin over Kamala Harris. In 2020, Biden beat Trump in the county by 17 percentage points.

In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five percentage points in 2024, despite a 13-point loss in 2020.

Voter Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old resident of Brownsville, assessed the two years since Trump took office as a “positive change”, with fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases to be processed.

Upon taking office, Trump declared a state of emergency at the border, staunching asylum claims in what rights groups say runs counter to US law. The US Supreme Court has since ruled that US border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil to claim asylum.

“A lot of people claim that they support illegals and want to let them in,” said Arizpe, a regular Republican voter, “but then, I say ‘well let them in your house’. And they don’t want to do it, right?”

On border policy, “at first, I supported Trump,” said Martin Torres, a 55-year-old who cast his ballot for Democrats at a public library in Brownsville as part of the state’s early voting.

But domestic enforcement, and its impact on the local workforce, soured his views.

“Now he changes everything,” he said.

A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.

Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Rights groups say the decision effectively allows racial profiling.

In Texas, a state law also lets local officials stop individuals they suspect entered the country illegally.

“I just see a lot of discrimination going on,” said George Castorena, a 46-year-old department of education worker, who said he was voting for change.

To be sure, midterm elections can only offer incremental change on an issue as entrenched as immigration enforcement and border policy.

Democratic control of the House of Representatives would at best serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration legislating more immigration enforcement funding and policy, while opening the door to investigations into the administration’s approach.

Control of the Senate, which could be determined by the contest between Texas Republican Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico, could further increase the party’s leverage.

A change in the governor’s office, meanwhile, could end Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s myriad uses of state agencies to support federal immigration enforcement. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa, if she were to pull off an upset, would be largely constrained by a likely Republican-dominated state legislature and a mountain of pre-existing law.

A galvanising moment?

Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.

A poll conducted by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas found that only 34 percent of respondents from the area felt that immigration enforcement by both local and state officials had made their communities safer. Fifty-three percent said it made their lives harder without improving safety.

Meanwhile, 64 percent felt ICE tactics have gone too far. The numbers broadly align with polls showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores in two Rio Grande Valley congressional districts.

Republicans, eyeing Trump’s success in 2024, viewed the races as strong prospects early in the election season.

“What this survey conveys is: people along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024,” Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at ACLU of Texas, told Al Jazeera.

Even prominent community figures who support Trump’s policies acknowledge a broader change in sentiment.

Eli Lara, the lead pastor at the non-denominational New Life Family Church in McAllen, Texas, said locals have been dismayed by the wide scope with which the administration has targeted undocumented individuals.

“The immigration issue is bigger because [the community] is seeing people being taken,” he told Al Jazeera. “I don’t like the separation of families, but here’s the thing: there are consequences for choices.”

That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.

“He’s been faithful [to the church] for two, three years, but they picked him up,” Lara said. “Why? Because he had a bad criminal record in the past. God forgives, but the government doesn’t.”

Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.

She pointed to several instances that have recently shaken the region, including the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in the town of Alamo in the Rio Grande Valley, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July 2026 in the Texas city of Houston.

“I’ve had a lot of people tell me, ‘Why do I care about politics? Politics doesn’t affect me,'” she said. “And with all of these ICE raids, they realise politics does affect them, and it sucks that it took a lot of trauma to really bring that to people.”

A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.

Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.

That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.

Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.

news.title: US Midterms: Democrats Are Pushing Into Republican Territory
news.text:
By Ashok Nilakantan Ayers

WASHINGTON: More than 39 million Americans have already voted. The Democratic candidates are campaigning on the cost of living, and US President Donald Trump is taking his fight into Republican strongholds. The early-voting surge signals intense engagement—but its political meaning remains uncertain.

As the United States enters the final stretch of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, the campaign has become a nationwide test of President Donald Trump’s political standing, the Republican Party’s congressional strength and the Democrats’ ability to turn voter dissatisfaction into electoral gains.

The numbers are already staggering attracting attention. More than 39 million Americans had cast their ballots early by October 28, according to the University of Florida Election Lab figures reported by Axios on October 29. That compares with approximately 46 million early votes during the entire 2022 midterm election period. The latest count represents a substantial advance in participation before Election Day, although it does not establish how many people will vote overall or which party will benefit.

The contest is unfolding against a backdrop of concerns about the cost of living, the administration’s policies and the economic and foreign-policy consequences of the Iran war. Democrats are seeking to make the election a referendum on the White House; Republicans are attempting to preserve their congressional majorities and prevent the president’s legislative programme from being obstructed during the final two years of his term.

The most visible feature of the closing campaign has been the geographical contrast between the two parties’ priorities.

Trump has been travelling extensively through states that he won comfortably in the presidential elections, while also appearing in battlegrounds where Republican candidates face serious challenges. According to ABC News’ tracking published on October 27, he had made 20 campaign stops in states he had won decisively and six in battleground states since September 9. Texas, Ohio and Tennessee have featured prominently in his itinerary.

For Trump, these appearances serve two purposes: mobilising his core supporters and lending his personal political capital to candidates whose races could determine control of Congress.

The president has repeatedly urged supporters to treat the election as a contest in which his own agenda is at stake. Although his name will not appear on the ballot, the outcome could shape the remaining two years of his presidency, affecting legislation, spending, investigations and the administration’s ability to advance its priorities.

Vice-President JD Vance has also been deployed to reinforce Republican campaigns. He was scheduled to visit North Carolina on October 28 for a rally in Kinston, having already returned to the state earlier in the closing campaign. He has also campaigned in states including Alaska, where Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces a competitive challenge.

The repeated visits to states that Republicans normally consider favourable reflect the importance of turnout and the uncertainty surrounding several races. A state can remain Republican leaning overall while individual Senate, gubernatorial or House contests become highly competitive.

The Democrats’ closing strategy is built around a different calculation: expand the electoral map, attract voters who do not normally participate in midterms and persuade independents that the administration’s record on household finances deserves scrutiny.

Former president Barack Obama has returned to the campaign trail, appearing in Georgia and Ohio to support Democratic candidates. On October 28, Obama was campaigning in Georgia alongside Senator Jon Ossoff, while Trump was in Ohio supporting Republican Senator Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The competing appearances illustrated how both parties are treating a handful of states as critical to the national contest. Former vice-president Kamala Harris has also campaigned for Democratic candidates, with recent appearances in Nevada, Mississippi and New Hampshire. Other prominent Democrats, including progressive lawmakers, are working to mobilise younger voters and voters concerned about economic pressures.

The Democrats’ message centres on affordability, the cost of everyday necessities and opposition to the administration’s handling of the Iran war. Republicans, meanwhile, are emphasising taxes, cultural issues and their opposition to what they describe as excessive government intervention. The contest is not simply between two campaign messages. It is also about which party can bring its supporters to the polls in sufficient numbers, particularly in states where congressional contests are close.

The most striking development is the number of Americans who have already voted. According to the University of Florida Election Lab figures reported by Axios, more than 39 million ballots had been cast by October 28. Approximately 20 million were cast in person and nearly 19 million by mail. The figures are provisional and change as states report additional ballots.

The early-voting total is substantial, but it is important to distinguish between a high early-voting count and a record overall turnout. The 2026 total is already approaching the entire early-vote count from 2022, with several days still remaining. Yet voters who cast their ballots early might otherwise have voted on November 3. The increase does not necessarily represent an equivalent increase in the total number of people who will vote.

There are nevertheless indications of heightened Democratic engagement in some important states. An ABC News analysis published on October 28 found that less-frequent voters in Texas and Georgia were participating at higher rates than at comparable points in the 2022 midterm cycle, with Democrats attracting a greater share of this group.

This matters because less-frequent voters can alter the composition of the electorate. However, early-voting statistics are not a direct count of votes for either party. In states that disclose party registration, registration identifies a voter’s declared affiliation, not the candidate for whom that person voted.

The 2026 election involves a vast electorate. A September estimate by the Pew Research Centre put the number of eligible voters at approximately 249.75 million American citizens aged 18 and above living in the 50 states and the District of Columbia. The estimate excludes certain groups, including eligible Americans living abroad, and is not the same as the number registered or expected to vote.

For comparison, the US Election Assistance Commission reported 234.5 million registered voters in the 2024 general election, including active and inactive registrations. That historical registration figure should not be mistaken for a verified 2026 registration count. The United States has no single, continuously updated national voter-registration roll that supplies a definitive current figure for every state.

The congressional stakes are equally clear: House of Representatives: all 435 voting seats are being contested, Senate: 35 seats are on the ballot, including regular elections and special elections, Governorships: voters in 36 states are choosing governors. These contests will determine the political balance of Congress and influence state-level policy for the next two years.

The early-voting surge is unusual, but the historical comparison requires care. The 2018 midterms produced turnout of approximately 48.1% of the voting-eligible population in House elections, according to Pew Research Centre’s analysis of official returns. In 2022, the comparable figure declined to about 45.1%, although turnout among citizens of voting age was higher under the Census Bureau’s separate methodology. These differences illustrate why the population used to calculate turnout must always be specified.

The 2020 presidential election recorded substantially higher participation than a typical midterm, as presidential contests generally attract a broader electorate. Early and mail voting also became much more prominent during the pandemic and have remained important since then. In 2022, approximately 47.1% of voters reported voting early, by mail or through a combination of those methods, according to the Census Bureau. That was lower than the extraordinary 2020 level but higher than in 2018.

There is no single meaningful national average that divides all Americans into those who vote on Election Day and those who vote early. States have different rules, voting periods and reporting practices. Moreover, the number of early votes is a count of ballots, while turnout percentages are calculated against a defined eligible or registered population.

Consequently, November 2026 cannot yet be described as a record-breaking election in overall turnout. The early-voting count is approaching the 2022 full-period total, but the final participation rate will not be known until after Election Day and the completion of official returns. The closing days will test whether Democratic enthusiasm translates into enough votes in competitive districts and states, and whether Republicans can mobilise the coalition that supported Trump in 2024.

For Trump and Vance, the campaign is about defending congressional majorities and demonstrating that the president retains the capacity to bring supporters to the polls even when economic concerns and disapproval of his policies complicate the political environment.

For Democrats, the challenge is to turn dissatisfaction into votes, defend vulnerable incumbents and make gains beyond their traditional strongholds. Obama’s return to campaigning adds national visibility, while candidates are also trying to connect the election to local concerns about prices, jobs, healthcare and public services. The early-voting figures offer evidence of intense participation and potentially shifting engagement among important voter groups. They do not, on their own, establish the final outcome.

On November 3, the decisive evidence will come from ballots counted across 435 House districts and the 35 Senate contests. The result will shape not only the balance of power in Washington but also the political constraints under which Trump governs for the remainder of his term.

For a president whose name is not on the ballot, the midterms are nevertheless a consequential measure of his administration’s political reach. For the Democrats, they are an opportunity to demonstrate whether their campaign message can convert voter concern into congressional representation. The early vote has raised the stakes; the final count will supply the answer. (IPA Service)

news.title: Maine lobster bill gets an assist from key Texas ally
news.text:
Senate Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz said his panel will take up legislation next month to extend a moratorium on new North Atlantic right whale protections, a move the Texas Republican credited to Maine GOP Sen. Susan Collins five days out from one of the most pivotal elections of her career. 

Collins, who is in a competitive reelection campaign against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, requested the committee take up the lobster industry-backed bill in a September letter with Sen. Angus King, I-Maine. 

Cruz wrote Thursday on X that Collins’ “leadership has been instrumental in advancing this bill to protect Maine’s lobstermen from burdensome regulations. I hope we can move this bill without changes or further delay to put on President Trump’s desk ASAP.”

The House-passed bill is a priority for the state’s lobster industry, which argues an extension of the moratorium, set to expire Dec. 31, 2028, for another seven years would provide greater certainty — particularly with the presidency up in the air in 2028.

Congress first imposed the moratorium in late 2022 at the behest of the Maine delegation on both sides of the aisle, inserting it into a year-end spending package.

The move came in response to a Biden administration “biological opinion” issued in 2021 recommending tougher restrictions to try to keep the endangered right whales from getting tangled up in commercial fishing lines — a major contributor to the population’s decline.

But the potential for major changes such as a mandate to use “ropeless” gear and fishery closures was too much for the Maine lobster industry, which fears a future administration could revive similar efforts.

To try to balance the concerns of environmentalists, the 2022 law appropriated $20 million to “support the adoption of innovative fishing gear deployment and fishing techniques to reduce entanglement risk to North Atlantic right whales,” part of an overall $280 million appropriated in recent years for right whale recovery efforts.

The Maine Department of Marine Resources has been using the congressionally appropriated funds to collect data for the past few years. Collins and King wrote last month that extending the regulatory pause would allow such efforts to continue and better inform future decisions.

According to the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, the industry supports about $2 billion in annual economic activity and 17,500 jobs.

“It is critical that any future regulatory actions appropriately balance protecting North Atlantic right whales with the economic and practical realities facing Maine’s lobster industry,” Collins and King wrote.

Tight margins

Compounding matters for the industry has been tariff-driven uncertainty and higher inflation.

In response to Trump administration tariffs, the Canadian government initially retaliated against a range of U.S. exports, including seafood; after Collins and others intervened, Canada walked those levies back.

Still, other tariffs and cost increases have hit the industry hard, said Curt Brown, president of Bold Coast Seafood in Prospect Harbor, Maine. “Our traps are built of vinyl-coated steel. Trap prices have gone up, bait prices have gone up, fuel prices have gone up. So margins are tight,” he said. 

Brown and other industry representatives say implementing greater protections for right whales would make matters worse, increasing costs and potentially forcing some lobstermen out of business. 

“I don’t think you will find any fisherman that says they want to harm a whale; we all support very healthy oceans,” said Virginia Olsen, executive liaison and political director for Maine Lobstering Union Local 207.

But Olsen, whose family has worked in the lobster business for five generations, said more time is needed to study the new data coming in through the Maine Department of Marine Resources’ research.

Hence the Trump administration-backed legislation introduced by Reps. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y. — another top midterm target of Democrats — and Jared Golden, D-Maine, who is retiring, to extend the moratorium through 2035.

It passed the House on Sept. 1, but not without opposition from most Democrats and even a couple Republicans sympathetic to the whales’ plight. The vote was 219-196, with 10 Democrats in favor and two Republicans opposed — Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Aaron Bean of Florida.

While Fitzpatrick has previously voted against his party on matters concerning endangered species, Bean represents Amelia Island, the winter calving and nursery ground for the whales. Amelia Island has its own cottage industry to protect, with the annual Right Whale Festival scheduled for next month. 

Aside from Golden and fellow Maine Rep. Chellie Pingree, other House Democrats who supported the measure include those in tough races in swing districts, such as Washington’s Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Texas’ Vicente Gonzalez.

Maggie Goodlander and Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, next door to Maine, also supported the bill. Pappas is running for Senate to replace the retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, against former GOP Sen. John Sununu; Inside Elections rates the race Tilt Democratic.

Lame-duck opportunity

With Democrats expected to make big gains next Tuesday, the lame-duck session may be the best chance for the bill’s supporters to get the bill enacted.

While Pingree is herself a senior Appropriations Committee member, the potential losses of Collins and Lawler, combined with Golden’s scheduled departure, could make it an uphill climb in the 120th Congress.

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates Collins’ and Lawler’s races each a Toss-up. 

The bill has already been an assist to Lawler, who has pointed to it as evidence of his ability to work across the aisle. His race is in a district former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024. 

Golden originally introduced his own bill that would implement an identical extension. Lawler, who represents a landlocked district in New York’s Hudson Valley, said he joined the effort through a desire to “fight for small business.” 

Golden returned the favor last month by endorsing Lawler in his hometown paper The Journal News, highlighting their cooperation on the bill.

The reasons for House GOP leaders taking up Lawler’s identical, separate bill have never been made clear; some speculate it simply has to do with ensuring the credit goes to a vulnerable Republican.

While a Senate Commerce markup could give the measure some momentum, the battle for floor time in November and December will be intense. Collins, the Senate Appropriations chair, could try to insert the bill into another year-end spending package, though her staff wouldn’t comment on legislative strategy.

‘False dichotomy’

The North Atlantic right whale, with a remaining population of roughly 380, has been experiencing what’s known as an “unusual mortality event” under the Marine Mammal Protection Act for the last decade. Over 20 percent of the whales have either been either killed or injured, largely due to entanglements in fishing gear and collisions with ships. 

Still, supporters of the bill point to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data showing an increase in the number of individual whales since 2020, and 2026 was the largest calving season since the beginning of the unusual mortality event. 

Jason Joyce, a lobsterman and director of advocacy for the New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association, said the numbers demonstrate the need for more data before new regulations are imposed.

“What has happened since the current pause was put into place is births are up and deaths are down, so we’re in a better position now than we were when they were going to overregulate us,” Joyce said. 

But Katherine Sayler, southeast representative for Defenders of Wildlife, said even with the recent growth the population is still down significantly compared to historical population levels. 

“We’re not even close to the 500 North Atlantic right whales that we estimated in the population approximately 20 years ago,” said Sayler. 

Dan Moss, senior government relations representative for Defenders of Wildlife, added that the bill would sideline the work of a team established by NOAA nearly three decades ago to address risk to whales, and that it effectively ignores a court ruling that found current regulations for right whales in lobster fisheries are insufficient under federal law.

Backers and opponents of the bill have focused on the potential for regulations requiring the use of ropeless gear to reduce whale entanglements.

In this system, there’s still rope to connect individual traps, however it lacks the vertical line that leads to a buoy. Instead it relies upon systems that remain submerged until the trap owner triggers them just prior to retrieval.

During House floor debate, Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif., argued that the federal government was “dragging its feet” on right whale regulations, including by de-prioritizing ropeless gear. 

Both Olsen and Joyce said there are significant safety concerns related to the design of ropeless gear, since crew could become entangled without a simple method to retrieve them as with conventional gear.

“If my crew is wrapped and entangled in that rope and goes overboard, in my panic, I have to stop, grab a tablet, log in, open the app, deploy the buoy, wait for the buoy to get to the surface, and then put it in my hauler,” Olsen said. “There’s no way that my crew is going to come up alive.”

But Sayler argued the bill creates “the false dichotomy that there cannot be coexistence between fisheries and whales at a time when they face so many threats.”

She said that right whales play an important role in the ocean ecosystem through the nutrients they create and “that they are worth having on the planet for their incredible intrinsic value.”

news.title: MATT CALKINS: Megan Rapinoe defends biological males in women's sports saying sports were not meant to be fair
news.text: There is a reason that Megan Rapinoe only does interviews with people she knows won't challenge her. It's the only way the former soccer star won't end up red-faced or storming off in a fit of rage. Her answers leave her too vulnerable. Her comments sit on the summit of Mindless Mountain. Her recent sit-down with comedian W. Kamau Bell proved as much. MEGAN RAPINOE SAYS WOMEN'S SPORTS ARE FACING 'REGRESSION' OF 'EQUAL RIGHTS' IN NEW KAMALA HARRIS INTERVIEW Among the topics the pair discussed was trans people in women's sports, which Rapinoe has been a staunch advocate for. Here's how it started. Bell: "There's a lot of talk about how damaging trans women are to sports, so I give you credit for not being afraid to stand with trans people of all types, but also trans women in sports." Rapinoe: "I am appalled, I think at just, like, the lack of basic humanity and empathy that people are showing and just the amount of fear and hate, and I just think the silence of athletes is a lot." WASHINGTON HS GIRLS BLAST MALE ATHLETE PARTICIPATING IN TRACK MEET: 'DON'T THINK THAT THAT'S RIGHT OR FAIR' Basic humanity and empathy? Fear and hate? One could just as easily argue — or better yet, more convincingly argue — that she lacks empathy toward the women and girls who are losing competitions or sharing locker rooms with biological males. Last week, I saw a girl forfeit her cross country season because she chose not to race against a boy. She wasn't giddy about this. She broke down in tears while hugging her mother. Does Rapinoe feel empathy for her? As for athletes being silent? Megan might want to take that as a sign. It's probably not that they're afraid to stand with her on this issue — it's that they likely disagree with her, as do most Americans. And unlike Rapinoe, who can't lose a spot to a male, these athletes are still active and under that threat. The interview continued. Bell: "Why aren't you afraid of trans women in sports? Because that's the big fear is that it's like, suddenly it's LeBron James with a wig on, blah blah blah." Rapinoe: "Yeah, and that example isn't happening, and I don't think it's ever going to happen. I think there's a lot that trans people have to go through. If you're a trans person in sports to even play, it's like you couldn't just say, one day, 'I'm a woman' and go play. That's not how it works." Excuse me, but ... HAHAHA. That is exactly what happened with the high school cross country runner in Camas, Washington. He started the year on the boys team, finishing 76th in a junior varsity race. Then he switched to the girls team, where he's won one varsity race and finished second in three others. And not that it should matter, but he hasn't seemed to do anything to try and present himself as a girl. Not even a name change. So, yeah, Megan — it's happening. Rapinoe continued with the pièce de résistance: "And for me, one of the biggest things is God forbid somebody be good at sports and have some sort of advantage — and, by the way, sports is not fair in any sort of way ever. Right?" Bell (clapping his hands): "Yeah, it's not meant to be fair." Rapinoe: "Yeah, what's fair?" Bell: "I always point to [the 7-foot-4 Spurs center] Victor Wembanyama. Is that fair?" DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER Rapinoe: "What does that mean, even? It's already not fair, and also, just like, it isn't the most important thing in the world over someone's human rights or getting to play or being cruel to people. I don't know. I've won everything at every level, and played, you know in sort of every competition, and I'm just kind of like, I'm the one who could speak to it. Like, I'm okay if God forbid a trans person play sports and they're halfway decent at it." Yes, Rapinoe has won at everything at every level and played in every sort of competition. But do you know what one of those competitions was? Her U.S. National team playing a group of 15-year-old boys from Dallas and losing 5-2. So, in that sense, she is uniquely qualified to speak to boys playing in girls sports. She knows they'll kick girls' behinds. But even more asinine is the notion that sports aren't meant to be fair — along with Bell's attempt to equate Wembanyama's natural advantages with those of a transgender athlete. If sports weren't meant to be fair, there wouldn't be rules or referees. There wouldn't be punishments for performing enhancing drug use, weight classes in boxing or age limits in Little League. There is always going to be someone who's the best — whether it be Usain Bolt, Michael Jordan or Michael Phelps. But exhibiting athletic supremacy isn't unfair. Allowing men in women's sports, on the other hand, defies the very reason we separate the sexes. Simply put: If there was no separation, women's sports wouldn't exist. Personally, I don't think Rapinoe actually believes what she's saying. She saw firsthand what those 15-year-olds did to the best women's international soccer team in the world.
