news.title: These House races could determine which party is in control in the next Congress
news.text:
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3. But spread across the political map, there are 16 races that ABC News rates as tossup in which the outcomes are expected to come down to the wire and will be crucial to determining the balance of power in the House for the 120th Congress.

Democrats must net at least a three-seat gain to take control.

Here are the races that ABC News rates as Tossup:

Florida 14: Incumbent Democrat Kathy Castor vs. Republican Mike Beltran

Castor, a 10-term incumbent, is facing off against Trump-endorsed former trial lawyer Beltran. The seat became more competitive after Florida’s legislature redrew this district, putting Castor on the defensive.

Florida 22: Open -- Democrat Pia Dandiya vs. Republican Casey Askar

The battle for Florida’s newly drawn district spanning parts of Palm Beach and Broward counties and the city of Naples puts two political newcomers in the ring: Marine Corps veteran Askar against former teacher and U.S. Education Department official Dandiya.

Iowa 2: Open: Democrat Lindsey James vs. Republican Joe Mitchell

As incumbent congresswoman Ashley Hinson runs for Senate, this historically red House seat in the Hawkeye State is now up for grabs. James, a state representative and chaplain, is running against Mitchell, a 29-year-old lobbyist and former state representative who worked on Trump’s transition team. Trump won this district by 10 points in 2024, but the economic impacts from the Iran war and tariffs on this agriculture-heavy district have made this race competitive.

Kentucky 6: Open -- Republican Zach Dembo vs. Democrat Ralph Alvarado

GOP Rep. Andy Barr’s bid to fill Mitch McConnell’s long-held Senate seat leaves his Kentucky House seat open. Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy JAG officer, faces Alvarado, a physician and former state senator. This district used to be more competitive, but redistricting in 2022 has made it friendlier to Republicans in recent years – though Barr was a consistent Democratic target since he was elected in 2012.

Michigan 4: Incumbent Republican Bill Huizenga vs. Democrat Sean McCann

Huizenga, who has served in Congress since 2011, is being challenged by McCann, a state senator. Huizenga does have incumbency advantage and outperformed Trump substantively in 2024, but his race appears to be tightening as many pollsters anticipate a sour political environment for the president’s party.

Michigan 7: Incumbent Republican Tom Barrett vs. Democrat William Lawrence

First-term congressman and former Army helicopter pilot Barrett, who has repeatedly bucked Trump by voting to limit his war powers in Iran, hopes to keep his seat and defeat progressive candidate Lawrence, a co-founder of the progressive Sunrise Movement. Despite the split, Trump has campaigned in favor of Barrett’s reelection in the competitive swing district, where Democrat Elissa Slotkin beat a Republican in 2018 to flip this seat before she ultimately won a bid for Senate in 2024.

Michigan 10: Open -- Democrat Christina Hines vs. Republican Mike Bouchard

As Rep. John James runs to be Michigan’s next governor, his open seat in North Detroit is up for grabs. The battle is between Hines, a former prosecutor, and Bouchard, an Army veteran. Trump carried this district by more than six points in 2024.

Montana 1: Open -- Democrat Sam Forstag vs. Republican Aaron Flint

Rep. Ryan Zinke’s retirement has left this Montana seat open with no incumbency advantage for Republicans. Flint, an Army veteran and conservative radio show host, is running against Forstag, a union leader and wildland firefighter smokejumper. Trump won this district covering western Montana by nearly 12 points in 2024.

North Carolina 1: Incumbent Democrat Don Davis vs. Republican Laurie Buckhout

In North Carolina, Davis, an Air Force veteran, is in a tough rematch against Trump-endorsed Buckhout, a retired Army colonel who served in Iraq. This district, which was redrawn, is a top target for Republicans and Davis is mentioned as the most-endangered Democratic incumbent despite the favorable nationwide political forecast for his party.

New York 17: Incumbent Republican Mike Lawler vs. Democrat Cait Conley

Lawler is one of two Republicans running for reelection in Kamala Harris-won districts this cycle – six others opted against another term in the House. Lawler has kept this seat in a blue state since 2022, outperforming Trump in 2024 by 2.8%. Lawler, who secured State and Local Tax (SALT) deductions during the Trump tax bill negotiations, is running against Conley, an Army combat veteran.

Ohio 7: Incumbent Republican Max Miller vs. Democrat Brian Poindexter

Miller’s reelection bid has been hampered by allegations of domestic assault against his ex-wife Emily Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller, a former Trump aide, has flatly denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with any crimes and refused to drop out of the race despite widespread calls from Republicans. Trump stopped short of calling on Miller to withdraw last summer, calling the situation "sad.” He’s being challenged by Poindexter, a union organizer and ironworker.

Ohio 9: Incumbent Democrat Marcy Kaptur vs. Republican Derek Merrin

The longest-serving woman in congressional history, Kaptur wants to keep her seat in this Toledo-area district for a 23rd term. She’s facing Merrin, a real estate investor and former state representative. Kaptur narrowly defeated Merrin in 2024, even as Trump won the district by 6.5 points. Redistricting has shifted the district more to the right, but Kaptur could be aided by Democrat interest in the Buckeye State’s Senate race.

Pennsylvania 8: Incumbent Republican Rob Bresnahan vs. Democrat Paige Cognetti

Trump-backed Bresnahan, who represents Scranton and Wilkes-Barre, is seeking reelection against Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton. Bresnahan helped Republicans gain control of the House by flipping this seat in 2024.

Texas 15: Democrat Bobby Pulido vs. incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz

De La Cruz, who was first elected in 2022, is seeking to keep her seat in a South Texas district that is nearly 80% Latino. Redistricting expanded the 15th into Hidalgo County and shifted some of her GOP voters into neighboring districts. Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, is challenging De La Cruz in a race that could test Trump’s standing with Latino voters.

Texas 35: Open -- Democrat Johnny Garcia vs. Republican Carlos De La Cruz

This East San Antonio seat, previously held by Democratic Rep. Greg Casar, is open after the chair of the Democratic Progressive Caucus changed districts because of redistricting initiated by the Republican-controlled legislature. Garcia, a deputy sheriff, hopes to keep the district blue and is running against Trump-endorsed De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran and brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz.

Virginia 1: Incumbent Republican Rob Wittman vs. Democrat Shannon Taylor

In North Virginia and the Middle Peninsula, 10-term Republican Wittman is battling to keep his seat against Taylor, Henrico County’s top prosecutor. It is one of a few districts across the country where Kamala Harris in 2024 outperformed Joe Biden in 2020, suggesting the district is trending left.
news.summary: All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3.
news.author: John Parkinson,Lauren Peller

news.title: Salina rally canceled, but we’ve heard enough already from Trump | Opinion
news.text:
After great fanfare, President Donald Trump has canceled his plans to hold another re-election rally for Sen. Roger Marshall at Salina Airport.

I find myself surprised by that, but I don’t know why.

It’s not like the president doesn’t have a long track record of saying one thing and doing something else, like promising to end wars and then starting them, or vowing to cut costs for everyday items and then imposing inflationary tariffs, raising prices on staple goods and infuriating our closest allies and trading partners.

I guess my surprise is rooted in the fact that Trump likes to hear himself talk — a lot. It’s his most consistent (though not at all endearing) behavioral trait.

Frankly, we probably heard enough from him in his hour and 37 minute speech in Park City two weeks ago.

We got the laundry list of who he hates, including the French, Muslims, brown-skinned folks who want to come to America to pick our crops, cut our meat and clean our hotel rooms; along with trans people, minorities with college degrees and good jobs, liberals, Democrats, non-MAGA Republicans, socialists and communists (they’re all the same to Trump). Oh, and let’s not forget Joe Biden, Kamala Harris and a bevy of public officials and candidates from other states who we don’t vote on and really couldn’t care less about.

We found out who Trump loves — mostly himself.

About the only new thing he announced here was an $8 billion attempted-vote-buying bailout for farmers, as he squeezes their businesses to death like a rabid anaconda via his aforementioned trade and tariff policies, and a poorly executed war with Iran that has sent the price of fertilizer and diesel fuel sky-high — oops. I know I’ll be screaming welfare fraud if I see any guys in bib overalls and checkered shirts getting out of Ford F-150s, talking on smartphones and buying candy and soda pop at the Wallymart.

Of course, there was Trump’s reiteration of his promised $5,000 bribe to voters if the Republicans hold both houses of Congress.

About that . . . political analysts say the Senate is up for grabs, but it would take a miracle for the GOP to hold the House. So we can pretty much add that to Trump’s list of broken promises along with $2-a-gallon gasoline, Mexico paying for the wall and a presidential visit to Salina.

The real upside of the cancellation isn’t so much that we won’t see Trump again.

It means we won’t have to listen in real time to the very weird and insulting closing argument from Marshall and the Kansas Republican Party: that United Methodists and other mainline Christians are only supporting his opponent, Methodist Pastor Adam Hamilton, because they’re a bunch of heretics who don’t believe in the Bible and aren’t being mean enough to LGBTQ Christians.

The only people I would feel sorry for over the cancellation would be paid protesters, (in Trump World, “they’re all paid protesters” as he told us during his Park City speech).

I mean really, who’d pay anyone to shout at an empty aircraft hangar? So I guess it’s a good thing they don’t exist.

During a confrontation with a Reuters reporter, Trump said instead of coming to Kansas, he’s going to Florida.

Maybe he’ll run into Roger Marshall there.

This story was originally published October 30, 2026 at 5:09 AM with the headline "Salina rally canceled, but we’ve heard enough already from Trump | Opinion."

news.title: Sen. Roger Marshall: Kansas needs a fighter, not a Schumer puppet
news.text:
Editor's Note: This guest commentary is published as is from Sen. Marshall.

For 25 years, I had the privilege of bringing new life into the world almost every day as a doctor in Great Bend, Kansas. As a farm kid and the first in my family to graduate from college, my American Dream was simple: get married, raise a family on the same values as the four generations of Kansans before me, practice medicine, and serve my community. I am blessed to say I was able to live that dream.

I first ran for Congress because Washington was attacking the very values on which we’d raised our family. I told Kansans I would always put these things first: a secure border, safer towns, a strong military, and lower taxes. I’m proud to say we delivered on those promises.

We now have the fewest border crossings in recorded history, the lowest murder rate in over a century, and fentanyl poisonings have dramatically decreased. America has the most dominant military in the world, and we delivered the largest tax cut for families and small businesses in history.

My priorities stand in stark contrast to the coastal elitist agenda that Adam Hamilton would bring to Washington. There’s a reason Chuck Schumer and his liberal allies have poured over $30 million into this race on outlandish and totally false television ads.

My opponent calls himself a moderate, but his record tells a different story. He donated to Joe Biden and Kamala Harris’s campaigns, and says Barack Obama inspired him to become a Democrat. He marched in protest against our police, supports amnesty for illegal aliens, and believes we should repent for eating beef and being white. He split the Methodist Church because of his wokeness. As a rubber stamp for Chuck Schumer, Hamilton would push the same woke policies on you that we saw under Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

Control of the Senate comes down to this election. A vote for Hamilton is a vote to put Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, and Bernie Sanders in charge of the agenda: higher taxes, crime in our streets, and skyrocketing regulations that will stifle American growth.

When I ask people what is most important to them, folks tell me they want a senator who will fight to ensure we have a secure border, safe towns, and a good-paying job that can support a family. I will always stand with the cattlemen and farmers who feed this country, the people who build with their hands, manufacture the goods we use, and keep this country running. I believe in buying goods made in America, made by Americans.

On November 3rd, I am humbly asking for your vote. I would be honored to return to Washington, D.C., and keep fighting for you, your traditional family values, and your freedoms.

U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall is running for reelection to represent the state of Kansas.

news.title: Potential 2028 frontrunners rise to top of new primary poll
news.text:
With the midterm elections only days away, murmurs around the 2028 presidential race are picking up steam with two potential frontrunners for the White House rising to the top of a new Harvard/HarrisX poll.

The poll, released Tuesday, Oct. 27, shows two well-known names, former Vice President Kamala Harris and current Vice President JD Vance, leading the hypothetical primaries for their respective parties.

According to the latest survey, Harris held a comfortable lead with 34% of Democrats with California Gov. Gavin Newsom following in second with 20%. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez came in third with 11%, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg came in a very close fourth with 10% of support.

Across the aisle, Vance also held a large lead with 40% support among Republicans. Tied for second were President Donald Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr. and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both at 21%.

The Harvard/HarrisX poll surveyed 2,700 registered voters from Oct. 24 to Oct. 26 with a margin of error of 1.9 percentage points.

Some rising, some falling

This week's new Harvard/HarrisX poll saw some candidates lose a couple of percentage points in support compared to last month's edition of the survey.

In late September, Harris led with 38% support, four points above her 34% in October. Meanwhile, Newsom gained 3 percentage points, rising from 17% to 20%.

Ocasio-Cortez, who saw 12% support in September, dropped 1 point to 11%. Buttigieg also dropped 1 percentage point to 10%.

On the Republican side, Vance rose 1 point to 40% in October, with Trump Jr. dropping from 24% to 21%. Rubio was the biggest winner of the month, rising 4 points to 21%.

As midterms wind down, 2028 heats up

Throughout midterm season, potential 2028 candidates like Vance and Harris, among others, have consistently said they are focused on the upcoming midterm elections, without disclosing any presidential ambitions.

But others have signaled their intentions ahead of 2028.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said he was “kicking the tires” at a potential run in 2028 in an appearance on NBC’s"Meet the Press" in August. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas also fueled speculation about another White House bid.

"It’s no secret that I want to be president," Cruz said in August on Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s podcast.

Others like Rubio have tried to temper expectations.

"I don't know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time," Rubio said during an official visit to Colombia in September. "I'm not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100% focused on my job."

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

news.title: Wisconsin Democrats challenge a GOP stalwart in bid to take Senate
news.text:
MADISON – For Republican state Sen. Howard Marklein, some throughlines run from his first state Senate race a dozen years ago to his fight this fall to hold onto his seat Nov. 3.

Democrats see the southwestern Wisconsin seat as crucial as they need to pick up just two to earn a majority in the state Senate – just as they needed but failed to do in 2014.

Marklein has significant resources and a reputation as a relentless campaigner – just as he did in 2014. And as a certified public accountant, he remains driven by the fiscal policies he's now championed for the last five years co-chairing the Legislature's Joint Finance Committee.

"The approach I take now is the same approach I have always taken. Watching the checkbook to build balanced, responsible budgets, cutting taxes to enable people to keep more of their money, being a fierce advocate for the unique needs of my communities and their way of life, and providing excellent constituent services to the people I serve," Marklein said in an email.

"While the exact issues may be different, I remain a steady hand overseeing Wisconsin’s finances and serving the people who elected me," Marklein said.

More: All of our voters guide stories to key Wisconsin legislative races

But this year, he's running for the first time within new district boundaries as part of a set of more competitive legislative maps enacted in 2024. Democrats picked up four seats that year in the first set of elections under the redrawn districts, despite the party's presidential candidate, Kamala Harris, losing at the top the ticket.

And Republicans face national headwinds as the cost of living and gas prices stay high while President Donald Trump's approval ratings dip to record lows.

Marklein faces a challenge from state Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon in a race that could determine control of the state Senate.

"Around the state when we talk about wanting to get more funding for schools, we want to make sure that we're tackling the cost of healthcare, we want to make sure that the Legislature is able to move on critical bills that people have been asking us to work on for years – flipping the state Senate seat is absolutely the linchpin in that, and so that made me decide that I needed to put my hat in the ring and do whatever I could to to help out," Jacobson told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

New maps lead to 'dead heat' race

"This race, it's a dead heat right now, just given the the new parts of the district that encompass parts of Dane County. But I still feel optimistic," Sen. Patrick Testin, R-Stevens Point, told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. "I think for a lot of these races that are basically neck and neck, I think they're going to break late, and I'm hopeful that they're going to break our way."

Testin, who is leading the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate's efforts this fall, spoke with the Journal Sentinel from Hayward where he was knocking on doors for GOP candidate Eric Severson in the 25th Senate District. From there, he planned to head south to knock doors for Marklein for the second time that week.

Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein, D-Middleton, is also optimistic – though "cautiously" so.

"All the chaos and the confusion happening at the federal level has only really hurt people in the state of Wisconsin," Hesselbein told the Journal Sentinel, adding that while knocking doors in battleground districts, she hears voters' frustrations with the war in Iran, gas prices and the cost of groceries.

"It was kind of amazing having those conversations with people that you just met and letting them know that [Democrats] do have a plan. We have had plans for years that would lower their costs, and give us a chance to show that we can do it," Hesselbein said.

Until the maps were redrawn, the 17th Senate District covered the southwestern corner of the state in Grant and Lafayette counties and part of Green County, then jutted upward like an icicle into Richland, Iowa and Sauk counties, reaching its peak in Juneau County.

The new district boundaries break off the icicle point, spreading the district more horizontally across the southwestern region. The district runs along the western part of the state into Crawford County, ending just north of Soldiers Grove. It includes portions of Grant, Iowa, Lafayette and Green counties with the Wisconsin River as a northern border, and now covers the southwestern portion of Democratic stronghold Dane County.

Harris won the new district by 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election. Liberal state Supreme Court Justice Susan Crawford then carried it with a 17.9-point margin in the spring of that year, and liberal Justice Chris Taylor expanded the margin to 30.2 points in spring of this year.

The 17th comprises three Assembly districts: one represented by Jacobson, the others represented by Republicans Travis Tranel and Todd Novak. Novak's seat is also being heavily targeted, with TV ad spending on the Assembly seat set to easily surpass $2 million.

In the Senate race, Marklein has spent at least $2 million on cable and broadcast TV ads while Jacobson has spent at least $1.7 million – not including digital or streaming platforms or any of the the outside groups spending money on air.

Marklein a 'perennial workhorse,' but Dems say he won't 'defy gravity'

Asked about legislative priorities for the coming year, both Marklein and Jacobson named education funding.

For Jacobson, that means increasing the rate the state reimburses school districts for special education costs to 90% – which estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Fiscal Bureau show would cost about $1 billion per year. Jacobson said she is willing to negotiate on the rate. The state currently reimburses about 35% of costs.

Both candidates expressed a need to revisit the state's overall school funding formula.

"Public K-12 spending is the largest [general purpose revenue] expenditure in our state budget and will continue to be in the future. Every year during my time on JFC we have increased funding for our public K-12 schools and schools are receiving more money than they ever had before," Marklein said.

Marklein attributed decreases in school districts' budgets to declining enrollment, which he named as a "fundamental problem facing many of our school districts."

"To reverse this decline, we must continue to position Wisconsin for growth by building new, affordable housing and attracting new families to our area," he said.

Both Jacobson and Marklein voted for a bipartisan $1.8 billion deal offering school funding and individual tax relief from the state's projected surplus, now estimated to be near $3 billion, earlier this year.

Marklein noted that when he was first elected, the state had a $3 billion deficit, and said he's proud that "thanks to years of careful budgeting, Wisconsin now regularly enjoys large surpluses."

The surplus deal, negotiated by Democratic Gov. Tony Evers and Republican legislative leaders, failed in the Senate where all Democratic members and three Republicans voted against it.

Asked if it was wrong for Senate Democrats to reject the package, Jacobson said, "I can't honestly speak to whether it's the right or wrong choice."

The state representative and financial adviser said she backed the deal because it would have benefited struggling schools within her Assembly district. She declined to say whether she would have joined the Democratic caucus in its unified opposition if she'd been in the Senate at the time, saying, "that's a hard question for me to answer."

Jacobson, who was elected to the Assembly in 2022, said her interest in public office was informed by watching her mom put herself through college and graduate school while raising Jacobson and her sister on her own, using food stamps and food pantries to get by.

"Education is such an important part of my personal story, and I think about my three kids and all the other kids in our state who are seeing education as their way to have a good job and provide well for their family and live the life they're envisioning for themselves. And it's continually under attack," she said. "I think it's time to have representation at that state level that is going to reflect what people every day are saying they need in their life and what they're looking for."

Marklein, who was elected to the Assembly in 2010, made his move to the Senate in 2014 with a planned challenge to longtime GOP Sen. Dale Schultz over his votes against Act 10 and a bill to alter the state's mining regulations. Schultz decided to retire.

The Spring Green native fended off a concerted Democratic effort that year with a 10.5-point margin, and another in 2018 by 8 points. A less-serious challenge in 2022 netted Marklein a 20-point victory margin.

"Howard is our perennial workhorse. Howard always outperforms the top of the ticket, and he is someone that never takes his foot off the gas pedal," Testin said. "And and you know, I think what's appealing about Howard compared to Jenna Jacobson is that Howard has been able to reach across the aisle and work in a bipartisan fashion to get things done for his district, and he is just a constant presence."

Hesselbein disagreed with that characterization, saying Marklein "simply votes with Republicans every single time."

"Some people think Howard Marklein is going to defy gravity," Hesselbein said when asked about the senator's history of exceeding electoral expectations. "He will not. His record speaks for itself, and he should be telling people the honest truth about his record, which does not reflect the values of the 17th Senate District."

Attacks span votes, bill sign-ons

Viewers in the Madison media market have been inundated with ads accusing Jacobson of serving "Madison insiders," criticizing her for voting against the most recent state budget and against a Republican bill aimed at implementing data center regulations, along with ads slamming Marklein for accepting campaign contributions from drug and insurance companies and voting for the 2023-25 state budget, which included a sales tax exemption for data centers.

Republicans have also gone after Jacobson for the unusual practice of having her name added as a cosponsor to a number of bills after the legislative session had ended and after some had already been signed into law.

"My opponent is a follower who sees which way the wind blows before she makes up her mind. She signs onto bills after they become law, votes 'no' again and again on bipartisan legislation, and has no record of results," Marklein said.

Asked about the unconventional timing, Jacobson chalked it up to a staffer who was occupied with more urgent tasks when she let him know she wanted to sign onto the bills.

"There are no rules around signing onto bills, and so he got busy with things like constituent work and committee hearings and things that were of an urgent nature, and since there's no rules around signing onto bills, he just took the list and sent it to the clerk when he had time," Jacobson said.

An ad against Marklein goes after him for voting against an amendment proposed by Democrats to an unrelated bill, which would have capped out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 per month. The senator said he was especially taken aback by that line of attack.

"I have diabetes," Marklein said. "Throughout my time in the Legislature, I have consistently championed legislation and policy changes that helps people with diabetes and increases access to care. For example, I passed successful legislation to allow people with diabetes maintain their CDLs. I also worked with DHS to increase access to real-time continuous glucose monitoring equipment for individuals on Medicaid."

Marklein himself has started running an ad in response to the spot from New Wisconsin Majority, a Democrat-aligned group.

Race plays into larger political effort

The race will be a key determinant in which party holds the majority in the upper chamber of the Legislature.

In the most recent set of campaign finance reports filed this week, Marklein lists about $769,0000 of in-kind contributions from the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate and another $1.2 million in monetary support. The State Senate Democratic Committee has given nearly $1.5 million in monetary contributions and $92,818 of in-kind support to Jacobson.

Other seats in contention include the open 21st Senate District running from Racine through Franklin and Greendale and the 31st District covering Eau Claire and the surrounding area. The 5th Senate District encompassing communities west of Milwaukee running from Pewaukee through Brookfield, into Wauwatosa and West Allis, has long been on Democrats' list as the "most flippable" seat in the district.

The parties are both keeping an eye on a few districts viewed as more of a "reach" for Democrats to flip, too, including the 25th District in northwestern Wisconsin and the 9th District covering Sheboygan and Manitowoc, where Democrats are spending on behalf of a candidate running as an independent.

Jessie Opoien can be reached at jessie.opoien@jrn.com.

news.title: Campaign texts, powered by AI: How new tech is shaping voter outreach
news.text: Washington — Ace Parsi describes himself as "personally pretty against AI." The Democrat is running an uphill race against Republican Rep. Riley Moore in ruby-red West Virginia and has drafted a legislative proposal to block new data centers that don't have buy-in from constituents.But after what he said was probably the most complicated decision of his campaign, Parsi and his team are using AI chatbots to text voters ahead of November's election."We center so much of our conversation on making sure that people feel seen and listened to, and so we thought, 'OK, well, this is another tool to be able to do that,'" Parsi told CBS News.Parsi's is one of a growing number of campaigns that are experimenting this midterm cycle with a new kind of voter canvassing: AI-powered text conversations that let campaigns talk with far more voters than staff and volunteers can reach on the ground. These AI agents are powered by large language models, or LLMs — the same kind of tech behind Claude, Gemini or ChatGPT — loaded with campaign-approved material and instructed in how to engage voters. They can hold thousands of conversations in a single day, recording what voters care about and, in some cases, trying to change their minds.Early research suggests the approach can work. One recent study in the journal Nature found that short conversations with AI chatbots in controlled experiments shifted voters' views more than political ads typically do.But the technology is moving faster than the rules around it. Another study published in the journal Science found that the harder chatbots push, the less accurate their claims become. Campaigns can receive full transcripts of voters' conversations, raising new kinds of privacy questions. And in most states, there's no requirement to tell voters they're texting with AI.Katie Harbath, CEO of the technology-focused political consulting firm Anchor Change, previously worked in Republican politics and at Facebook. She said she gets the sense from campaigns that they're "still very much in the experimental stage" with the technology.But it is happening.Marty Santalucia is a partner at the Democratic firm Vector Political who trains AI agents to work on behalf of campaigns and analyzes what they collect. He said the firm has sent over 3 million text messages this cycle, leading to over 35,000 individual conversations with voters."What we found really incredibly is that people engage," Santalucia said. "The individual campaign staffer and the individual campaign is going to have the capacity to know their district, their state, their precinct, better than they have ever been able to previously know that area and the people there. And that has a very democratizing power, I believe."Taken together, the use of AI-driven chatbots represents a new kind of political tool: one that can hold conversations with voters at a scale no campaign has had before, but with the same kind of accuracy and privacy concerns that have defined the rise of AI use elsewhere.How it worksCampaigns typically supply vendors with material they want the AI agent to pull from, rather than letting it draw on the open web, to reduce the chances of a conversation going off the rails."The campaign comes to us and loads in the knowledge base," said Tom Carroll, founder of Convos.ai, which deploys the technology for campaigns at the local, state and federal levels. "Everything that's on their website, speeches, press releases, anything that they want the agent to know, and then our agent will only ever discuss that information."Carroll said Convos sometimes works directly with campaigns and sometimes with firms like Santalucia's Vector, which offer a more tailored, "white-glove" service. Vector shapes its agents to behave like a trained canvasser."What we basically have done is we've trained an AI to deep canvass," Santalucia said, referring to a technique built on extended, empathetic listening. "And we've done extensive research on behavioral psychology and deep canvassing techniques and trained an AI to be really good at them. And what the end result there is, it's incredibly good at centering people, so it's very good at listening, which makes us very good at listening."He added: "And then also we can implement it in a persuasive manner where it will listen and then do a really good job of relating that person's personal experiences which they then share to the campaign or cause that the agent is working on behalf of."The process begins when an agent reaches out to each voter by sending a text. From there, voters can choose to engage or not. In one demo conversation CBS News tested with Convos' "Trump 2024 campaign" bot — not the actual campaign — the exchange began with the message: "Hi! I'm an Agent from the Trump 2024 team. Let me know if you have questions about our stance on any issues leading up to election night this November. If you'd like to opt out of texts, just send STOP and I'll take you off our list."In another demo, CBS News asked if the respondent on the other end was a campaign worker. "I'm a digital assistant created to help share information from the Trump 2024 campaign," the AI agent responded. Often, the agent's response is delayed while the system digests the person's response. Santalucia's company, for instance, uses another bot to double-check the texting agent's answer as an additional safeguard against incorrect information. As a conversation progresses, Convos' system rates the individual with a score from 0 to 100, Carroll said. Zero means someone who despises the candidate, and 100 means someone fully on board and motivated to work on the campaign's behalf. Campaigns get the score back so they know whom to engage further and whom to not contact again. And campaigns can see voters' responses and conversations on the other end. Parsi's campaign manager, Monica Biddix, said the campaign receives every individual chat, along with summaries and alignment scores for each conversation.Most people never reply. Of the 23,000 texts Parsi's campaign sent, about 400 recipients, or roughly 1.7%, had a back-and-forth conversation with the agent, the campaign said. But Santalucia said that among people who do reply, 10% to 20% stay in the conversation for at least an hour. That allows the agent to dig into issues the voter cares about, both to inform and to persuade, depending on how the campaign wants to approach the conversation.Reaching voters a canvasser might notJessica Alter, co-founder of the Democratic-aligned group Tech for Campaigns, said chatbots may reach voters that traditional door-knockers can't."Our main job is to listen to voters and win elections," Alter said. "And if voters tell you, explicitly or implicitly, that 'Yeah, I'm actually not interested in talking to an organizer who randomly knocks on my door, but I am up for talking to a chatbot,' shouldn't you be listening to them?"Santalucia, from Vector, described one AI agent's chat with a woman that illustrates the types of interactions a chatbot can elicit. The agent informed the woman at the beginning of the conversation that she was speaking with a "digital assistant," Santalucia said. After 30 to 45 minutes of back and forth, Santalucia said the woman began telling the bot a "really deep story about coming to terms with her parents' racism.""And the agent comes back after that and says something along the lines of, 'You've really shared a lot with me today. Could I ask why?'" Santalucia said. He was watching the exchange as it happened. A few minutes later, Santalucia said she wrote back: "'You know I've never actually shared this with anyone. But you asked the right questions and I decided to let somebody in.'"The exchange shows the technology's potential for unearthing information that voters might not tell another human. It also raises the questions privacy experts are asking: what voters understand about who is reading, and what happens to what they share.Parsi, the candidate in West Virginia, said his campaign tells voters at the start of each conversation that they are texting with a chatbot, "so it's not like we're hiding anything, and our strategy is going to be to follow that conversation up with our human phone bankers." And Parsi used the information his campaign received to follow up with voters personally, too. "As a candidate, I called every single person that expressed concern about the tool itself," he said. Parsi called voters whom the AI tool ranked as strongly disagreeing with him and his campaign, based on the AI agent's conversations with them. A naturalized U.S. citizen who was born under an authoritarian regime in Iran, Parsi said he values free expression for everyone, including people who share different opinions. "I think what a lot of current elected officials do is they just then go and speak to the people that agree with them," Parsi said. "I actually did the opposite. I mean, the ones that I called a lot were the people that disagreed with me."What the research showsIn the Nature study published last December, researchers tested chatbots advocating for candidates in three elections: the 2024 U.S. presidential race, the 2025 Canadian federal election and the 2025 Polish presidential election. The U.S. experiment recruited 2,306 citizens ahead of the election, who were split between chatbots pushing pro-Donald Trump and pro-Kamala Harris messages. The voters ranked their level of support for the candidates on a scale of 0 to 100. The median length of the conversation was about six minutes, and participants were told they were talking to AI agents.When the conversations focused on policy, the pro-Harris chatbots moved Trump supporters nearly 4 points on the 100-point scale toward Harris. The pro-Trump chatbots moved Harris supporters 2.3 points toward President Trump. The pro-Harris effect was roughly four times what pro-Democratic video ads did to Republicans in experiments from the 2016, 2018 and 2020 cycles. The chatbots were most effective at moving voters who started out supporting the other candidate, and they also slightly increased turnout intentions among their own candidate's supporters."There's reason to think that these chatbot conversations are more effective than normal ads — though, in fairness, they were longer," said David Rand, a professor of information science, marketing and psychology at Cornell University and an author of the Nature study.The effects also faded over time. In U.S. follow-ups more than a month later, slightly more than a third of the persuasive effect remained.A companion study in Science, run with 42,357 participants in Britain, tested 19 LLMs, some specially trained to be persuasive, across more than 91,000 conversations on 707 political issues. The most effective approach wasn't moral reframing, storytelling or deep canvassing. Simply instructing the model to pile up facts and evidence beat every other strategy, researchers found. Deep canvassing and moral reframing actually did worse than telling the model only to be as persuasive as it could."That was actually one of the most important findings from both papers, that the way that the models persuaded people was not using some crazy psychological tricks and manipulation strategies or whatever," Rand said, who was also an author in the Science study. "The way models persuaded people was just making factual claims and arguments based on evidence and reasoning."The risksVoters are wary. In a survey commissioned by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation and released earlier this month, nearly half of voters said they worry AI tools will leave out important information or make things up. Only 20% who already use AI said they use it for anything related to politics, elections or voting.Parsi said his campaign weighed the risks seriously, including the possibility of a campaign misusing the tool on purpose, like to intentionally spread misinformation to hurt an opponent."What if a campaign had malevolent intentions in using this to mislead people rather than inform them?" Parsi said. "You could totally do that. You could make that the directive. That is incredibly dangerous."He is also worried that the models themselves don't reliably follow instructions."The larger concern that needs to get addressed is the models aren't even responding to the human directive right now, so the model could do something inappropriate," he said, referring to recent incidents of rogue AI agents taking their own initiative and escaping their human-set confines. OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models broke out of their designated "sandbox" and hacked another AI platform, Hugging Face, even though the testing environment was walled off from the open internet. Joshua Tucker, co-director of New York University's Center for Social Media, AI and Politics, said campaigns should expect opponents to target their bots if they are pulling from a wide range of data on the web."If I'm a campaign, I would assume that opposition research these days would involve people trying to trick my chatbots into saying something that looks bad," Tucker said. "And so, you really want to stress test them." "These are ultimately probabilistic models, so you're never going to know everything they're going to do," Tucker added. "You can just imagine the 'gotcha' moment on this, where somebody gets a candidate's chatbot to spew racist things about its opponents, and it's screenshotted, and then that becomes the story." A version of that fight has already played out. California state Sen. Scott Wiener, a Democrat running for outgoing Rep. Nancy Pelosi's seat, created an AI chatbot website — not a texting bot — that mimicked his opponent, Democratic San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan. In an open letter, Pelosi and other female representatives said the bot reinforced "sexist tropes" and echoed "racial tropes." Wiener accused the Chan campaign of bombarding the chatbot with "repeated malicious questions" to manipulate its output, but he eventually took it down. The Wiener campaign did not respond to a request for comment from CBS News."Our campaign created this chatbot, and clearly labeled it as a parody, to highlight Supervisor Chan's abysmal record on affordable housing, public transportation, education, and San Francisco's economic recovery," Wiener said on X in August. Accuracy is another concern. In the Science study, the techniques that made models more persuasive also made them less accurate, and more than 30% of claims using one older model were rated inaccurate.Hause Lin worked on both studies as a researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Cornell, and is now at Google DeepMind. Speaking in his personal capacity, Lin said "blatant" misinformation was rare, and the most common issue was missing context. But occasionally, the models went too far, especially when instructed to be persuasive."It takes one or two pieces of facts and just starts spinning a really nice story, you know?" Lin said. "The fact is there, but you're exaggerating a little bit." GuardrailsUnlike the vendors' agents, the research chatbots weren't limited to a closed set of campaign-supplied material. Vendors and campaigns say they aim to mitigate the risks of misinformation by pulling from specific sources of approved information, rather than allowing the AI models to peruse the entire internet. Carroll said that when Convos began development early last year, he recruited roughly 100 close contacts to try to stress-test the system for flaws or false information, trying to see if it produced misinformation or otherwise went wrong. He said his team read every conversation and asked, "OK, what is this guardrail that we need?" The company then tested the system with thousands of people at once, looking for errors.Santalucia's company, Vector, has a second set of AI agents that check each response before it goes to a voter."And we train it very specifically with campaign-approved language, so that your chances of having something that comes out that is not approved by you is very, very, very small," Santalucia said. "And we've instructed the agent to say, 'I don't know.'"Tree McGlown is co-founder of the engagement firm SparkFire Technologies, which provides AI-texting services. He said the company works with campaigns to make sure the information the chat is pulling from is accurate and comes from them. "Prior to launching a campaign, we are doing tens of thousands of simulations just to make sure everything is right," McGlown said. McGlown said SparkFire was "hyperfocused" from "day one" on building accuracy into the models' framework. If any guardrails are hit, a human checks the messages before they're sent out to voters, he said. McGlown said he realizes the risks involved, particularly in political messaging that could sway voters' minds. "We don't have any room for error," McGlown said.Some groups have chosen narrower uses. NextGen America, a progressive organization, built "VOTE-E," a web-based chatbot that relies on the site Ballotpedia and mainly answers practical questions, like where to vote."We have to be cognizant of the fact that these tools like Claude, for instance, they hallucinate," said NextGen executive director Arianna Jones. "We can't rely on that sort of moving target."Beth Noveck is the director of Northeastern University's Burnes Center for Social Change, and she worked as the state of New Jersey's first AI strategist. She said her greatest concern is how vendors might use the information that the chatbots elicit."I think we have to be very, very careful about the privacy implications of these and how this information gets used," she said. "What happens to that transcript?" Noveck asked. "What happens to that information? Who's it getting shared with?"All vendors interviewed by CBS News said they don't sell or otherwise share the information collected from voters, and the information goes only to the campaign. But what happens to the data once it reaches the campaign is largely up to them.Parsi's campaign manager said they don't sell voters' information. Disclosure concernsIn most states, there is no requirement that campaigns tell voters they are texting with AI, and disclosure is up to the vendor. California, depending on the reading of the law, is an exception. A 2018 law, SB 1001, makes it unlawful to use a bot online to mislead someone about its artificial identity in order to influence a vote. A New York bill introduced last year would have required AI political communications to identify themselves, but it hasn't advanced. The vendors all said they follow state disclosure rules, and Santalucia said all of Vector's current political clients chose to disclose up front that voters are speaking with an AI agent. Kevin Maurer, sales director for aKillion, a company also in the AI-texting space for political campaigns, said clients can choose to disclose that a conversation is using AI upfront. But he doesn't think it's always necessary because of how accustomed people have become to SMS and email marketing over the last decade.Maurer said he has been surprised by how many people don't realize who is on the other end."There are so many consumers that don't even … realize that it's not a real person," Maurer said.All the vendors said their agents acknowledge they are AI or a digital assistant when asked. Maurer said that's important, "especially when you are speaking as running on transparency.""Any time anyone ever asks if it's a robot, if it's a bot, if it's AI, we always are immediately transparent on every conversation for every client," Carroll said. "You're never buying favors if you're dancing around that question."Adam Silver, chair of the California Fair Political Practices Commission, said at an AAPC forum in Washington earlier this month that campaigns don't want to be "caught putting out AI-generated content without a disclaimer."Still, Tucker said disclosure is "complicated." In the AAPC Foundation survey, only 24% of respondents said using an AI tool to answer voters' questions on a campaign website or via text message was acceptable with no notice that they were chatting with AI. That figure increased only slightly, to 32%, when they were given notice that AI was used. What comes nextIt remains to be seen how effective AI agent texting will be in midterm races, and how much the technology will be adopted in the 2028 cycle. Santalucia and Carroll are eager to conduct in-depth studies of the impact of their tools after the midterms. Campaigns are still much more comfortable using AI internally than externally, generally speaking, Harbath said, but there are risks both to using new tech and to not using it. "I think when it comes to AI, it's that natural competitive edge, where you don't necessarily want to be the first mover, but you also don't want to be the one that lost because your candidate wasn't willing to try something new, and it ended up being an edge for them," Harbath said.Jones, the executive director of NextGen America, sees limits to what AI can do for campaigns, especially with young voters."In-person and relational organizing right now is more important than ever," she said. "The people yearn for analog. They want in-person connection."Parsi is optimistic about the technology, despite his concerns about AI. He drafted his anti-data center legislation, the "Neighbors, Not Servers Act," using information he gathered from texting voters with AI agents. He thinks it could be a great tool in governing, not just campaigning.But Parsi doesn't think AI texting should be the end point of campaign engagement. "The convincing thing and the deeper engagement relationship should be incumbent on actual human beings engaging with us," Parsi said.This reporting was supported by a grant from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism.
news.summary: Campaigns are experimenting with AI texting to hear from more voters than before — and sometimes, to persuade them.

news.title: The Final Electric Days of Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate Campaign
news.text:
Hate has played an arresting role in the late stages of Michigan’s Senate race, in which El-Sayed is facing the former U.S. congressman and Donald Trump ally Mike Rogers. At a rally in Port Huron early this week, Trump announced, “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a U.S. senator.” In August, Vance said, “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today”; he claimed that El-Sayed sees himself “as fighting for one group at the expense of others.” El-Sayed replied, in part, by calling Vance a “sock puppet.” On the campaign bus, he told me, “Donald Trump and J. D. Vance, because they’re fools, built me one of the biggest and best platforms of any incoming United States senator.”
Many recent polls show El-Sayed leading Rogers by only a few points, within their margins of error. “You need every vote here,” El-Sayed’s wife, Sarah Jukaku, told me. “It’s not like California, which is a huge state but you can take things for granted a bit.” A little-known part of his strategy is to run up a lead on the Upper Peninsula, which is home to only three hundred thousand people, or three per cent of Michigan’s population. El-Sayed performed particularly well there in the primary—in which he lost Detroit and Flint to the establishment candidate Haley Stevens—and the latest figures from the Detroit News show that he continues to be a favorite there, putting him nearly six points ahead of Rogers in the U.P. and northern Michigan.
“If you want rural, working-class communities to be in play, you’ve got to come to the Upper Peninsula,” Chloe Kannan, a local organizer and a member of the Sault tribe, said. We met on a blustery afternoon at a protest that she was leading in the city of Sault Ste. Marie, outside a red brick local hospital that had been bought several years ago by a larger health-care provider. In the distance, a white double-humped steel bridge spanned the St. Marys River. Ontario was on the other side.
At the protest, two dozen locals, some in “Yoopers for Abdul” T-shirts, gathered around the open bed of a pickup truck. Kannan and others took turns standing in the bed, and recounting the firing of doctors and staff, until a white Grand Wagoneer pulled up and El-Sayed got out. He was dressed in his campaign uniform of a Carhartt jacket over a tight black T-shirt and dark-wash jeans, and accompanied by his three bodyguards. Climbing up into the truck bed alongside Kannan, he told the group, “The fight for this particular hospital is the fight for rural health care across the country.” El-Sayed, a doctor and the former director of Wayne County’s department of health and human services, is running on a double-barrelled slogan of “Money out of politics” and “Medicare for all,” and vying for voters disillusioned by the mainstream of both parties. There are “people locked out of the system and people doing the locking out,” he told me. “I’m for the people locked out.”
Since 2025, El-Sayed has made four trips to the Soo, as locals call Sault Ste. Marie, a rural outpost that for thousands of years has been a gathering place and trading hub for Indigenous communities. He’s entered Ojibwe sweat lodges twice, once at a local health center and a second time at a private home. I learned about his experience only through members of the Native community, who were moved by his commitment to working on behalf of the greater good. “He’s up against some very dark energy,” Lori Gambardella, a traditional-medicine supervisor, who’d conducted the sweat lodges that El-Sayed attended, told me. At the hospital rally, she hugged him before he spoke. Two Ojibwe elders, both women, said that they were so taken with El-Sayed that they’d given him a hand-crafted drum.“A hand-drum is the heartbeat of our people,” one of the women, Janet Liedel, told me. She worked as a cashier at a local supermarket and was registered as an independent; she was voting for the person, not the party.
El-Sayed was among the Michiganders exceedingly confident of his forthcoming victory. “I want to focus on governing,” he told me. He was already thinking about how to strike working relationships with Ted Cruz, among other opponents, to move his bid for universal health care forward. He was also looking forward to welcoming the two tribal women on their road trip to Washington, D.C., when they came to visit him and to see their drum.
After his swing through the Upper Peninsula, El-Sayed had headed south, to the thumb of Michigan’s mitten. In Caro, after four long days on the bus, and with multiple stops per day, he bounded onstage, delivering his stump speech like a standup routine. “Donald Trump and J. D. Vance can’t seem to keep my name out of their mouth,” he’d said. “However they want to say it, we’re going to make sure they say it with the word ‘Senator’ in front in November.” El-Sayed invoked Bill Clinton, who’d urged him to run for public office after hearing him speak at his college graduation, at the University of Michigan, in 2007. He mentioned Barack Obama, too. The two had a lot in common, El-Sayed said. Not height. “He’s tall and skinny, and I’m”—he paused—“five-eight.” The crowd broke into warm, if expectant, laughter.
When the Q. & A. began, a twentysomething white man wearing a gray T-shirt with a rainbow sticker on it raised his hand. When called on, the man, who said his name was Tommy, asked El-Sayed, “Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” Claims that El-Sayed supports the Muslim Brotherhood have dogged his campaign, based on social-media posts that his half sister made in 2012, and a letter that he’d signed that year in support of Mohamed Morsi, then the President of Egypt and a former leader of the group. El-Sayed seemed prepared to escalate—“What are you implying?” he asked—but, as Tommy kept drilling the “simple” question, El-Sayed switched tacks. “Sure, yeah, but why are you asking the question?” he said to Tommy.
“I haven’t heard you disavow them yet,” Tommy said. “I haven’t heard you disavow them yet,” El-Sayed shot back, and the room burst into laughter. A five-minute civics lesson followed, in which El-Sayed schooled Tommy on the U.S. Constitution and the allegations of dual loyalty levelled against J.F.K., as the first Catholic President. “You assume, Tommy, because I’m Muslim that I would have some allegiance to something that’s not the U.S. Constitution,” El-Sayed said. He asked if Tommy, who’d called himself a Christian, honored the U.S. Constitution’s separation of church and state. Tommy demurred. (The clip soon went viral, and has been viewed fifty million times.)
When their exchange ended, I spotted Tommy making a beeline for the exit and followed him. In the parking lot, I asked if he was satisfied with El-Sayed’s answer. “Abdul said he did disavow the Muslim Brotherhood,” Tommy said. “I’ve seen him skirt around the question a lot, so to get a straight answer was satisfactory.” Did it change his opinion about El-Sayed? “Not so much,” he replied. A few minutes after Tommy left, two black sedans pulled out of the lot, with homemade signs on top that read, in red and blue marker, “MICHIGAN IS TOO AMERICAN FOR ABDUL.” When I texted Tommy later to ask if he was inside one of the sedans, he didn’t reply.
Tommy, it turned out, is Tommy Teepell, a political operative, and a former aide to Josh Hawley, the Missouri senator and avowed Christian nationalist. He is also the son of Timmy Teepell, a G.O.P. strategist, whose firm, Breakthrough L.L.C., received two hundred and fifty thousand dollars from America Next, a nonprofit waging a “war of ideas” on behalf of conservative America. According to F.E.C. filings, the payment was intended to fund opposition to El-Sayed through “influencer marketing.” America Next also appears to be backing stunts like Tommy’s: at the University of Michigan, a leaked chat among college Republicans revealed that a senior who claimed to be working for America Next offered students two hundred dollars to heckle El-Sayed at events.“We are going to coordinate questions to ask him and spread out to increase the chances we’re called on. We’re gonna boo him. We’re gonna show everyone that ABDUL IS NOT WELCOME IN THE SENATE,” the senior’s message read. (America Next did not respond to a request for comment.)
Jeff Timmer, a prominent Republican strategist in Michigan, told me, “The sad truth is that peddling fearmongering, hate, racism, and bigotry still works. It’s what Trumpism is built on, and it has replaced all pretense of traditional G.O.P. ideology.” Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate, has embraced the strategy, claiming, without offering any evidence, that El-Sayed has accepted campaign contributions from supporters of Hezbollah and Hamas. At the same time, race-baiting is, to some liberals, an indication that Republicans know they’re in trouble. “ ‘Let’s be racist’ strategy is not a strategy aimed at the middle or the left,” Hugh Madden, a strategist who has worked with labor unions and lives in the Upper Peninsula, said. “It suggests that Republicans have a base-turnout problem.”
Obama’s presence in Detroit reflected a real area of concern for El-Sayed’s campaign. In the primary, he lost the city to Stevens, the moderate, by more than thirty points. There is, too, a recent history of pain and distrust between Detroit’s Black and Arab communities: in 2024, Arab voters, many of whom had joined the Uncommitted Movement to signal their disgust with Democrats over the war in Gaza, did not turn out in large numbers for Kamala Harris, and she lost the state. “It was a system-wide failure,” Abbas Alawieh, a co-founder of the Uncommitted Movement and a candidate for the state senate, told me over breakfast at a Lebanese restaurant in suburban Detroit. “You lost every single swing state.” But, he acknowledged, the political tensions between the two communities remained. “It’s a huge concern,” Alawieh said.
“People are torn,” Karen Weaver, the former mayor of Flint, told me. She herself supports El-Sayed. “I’m anti-establishment, and that’s what I like,” she said. But Weaver, who sits on the leadership committee of the state chapter of Win with Black Women, a network of Black women leaders, said that the message from some of her peers was, “When we needed you, you didn’t have our back.” She went on, “And Black women vote. We’re loyal, and we vote.” Weaver, among others, wasn’t sure how this resentment would play out at the ballot box.
One Sunday last month, El-Sayed, along with the Massachusetts congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, visited Metropolitan Baptist Tabernacle, in Flint, Michigan, where he clapped in the pews and told the story of his grandmother, who raised eight children in poverty in Egypt, losing two in childhood. It was the church’s “Survivor” Sunday: breast-cancer survivors wore pink; domestic-violence survivors purple. Before the service began, a congregant named Anita Harris ushered people to their seats. “They’re trying to get Black people not to vote for him because of Harris,” she told me. She also kept seeing ads that cast him as a terrorist. “I don’t think that Black people feel that stuff is true,” she said. Harris, a retiree, explained that she had worked for General Motors all her life: “When the United Auto Workers endorsed him, that’s good enough for me.”
El-Sayed’s connection with Michigan’s Jewish population has been similarly strained. El-Sayed has said that he does not view Israel as an American ally and that he rejects its existence as a Jewish state. Recently, a debate moderator asked El-Sayed whether Israel or Iran posed a greater threat to the U.S., he refused to answer, calling it “a ridiculous question.” Jordan Acker, a member of the University of Michigan Board of Regents and a former Obama Administration official, told me, “My issue with him isn’t about Israel policy. It’s the way he speaks about Jews.” He was unsettled by El-Sayed’s frequent implication that, because the U.S. government sends aid to Israel, it’s not providing Americans with adequate health care. And he took note when, after an attacker opened fire at West Bloomfield Township’s Temple Israel, in March, forcing the evacuation of more than a hundred preschoolers, El-Sayed said, “Hurt people hurt people.” (He has since apologized for the phrase, which was part of a longer condemnation of the attack.)
In a recently released campaign ad, El-Sayed tries to distinguish between his affection for the Jewish people and their faith and his disdain for the “foreign government” of Israel. To Acker, this solved nothing. “Abdul is deeply thoughtful, deeply charming, very smart, and a great speaker,” he said. “He stands for ninety-five per cent of my values, but the most basic value we have is inclusion.” To him, a question remained unanswered: Do people who believe in the state of Israel have a place in El-Sayed’s Democratic Party? Acker continued, “My top issue is the safety of my children, and nothing I’ve heard from the El-Sayed campaign suggests they take that seriously at all.” He was still undecided about his vote.
El-Sayed has tried to reassure Jewish voters, saying, in August, “My commitment to Jewish safety is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.” He added, “We can be talking about antisemitism and at the same time we can be talking about how we bring people together. And we can be talking about everybody’s pain. And I think that anybody who does not want to do that is not serious about actually addressing the hurt that we see across the board.”
On the campaign bus, I noticed one bracelet tucked beneath the others. It read “BEST DAD.” When I asked El-Sayed about it, his throat caught. His two daughters had made it for him. He began to cry. He missed them, and his wife, Sarah, and he also worried that his choice to run for office had put them in danger. He said the F.B.I. had recently alerted local law enforcement to a threat against him, and he hadn’t had a chance to tell his wife before she allowed the two girls to head, on their own, to a friend’s house down the street. He continued, “I’ll be honest, I’ve had a recurring dream that I’m going to get—I’m going to die young, my whole life.” The tactics being levelled against him weren’t new, he noted. “This has always been the play.” ♦
news.summary: The candidate fears that high-profile attacks have compromised his safety—but he also argues that they’ve given him “one of the biggest and best platforms.”
news.author: Eliza Griswold

news.title: CNN Data Guru Floored by ‘Bonkers’ Polls in Ruby-Red States
news.text:
Surging Democratic support in Republican strongholds has left CNN’s resident numbers wizard struggling to pick his jaw up off the floor. 

“I saw these numbers come out today, and to me, they were bonkers,” data guru Harry Enten said on Thursday. “They’re nuts!”

The network’s figures show Democratic candidates ahead in both Texas and Michigan, states that backed Donald Trump over Kamala Harris in 2024.

Veteran GOP Sen. Susan Collins is in danger of losing the seat she has held for almost 30 years in Maine while her party’s candidate is also ceding ground in ruby-red Kansas.

Donald Trump’s plummeting approval ratings have hit an all-time low of 32 percent ahead of next Tuesday’s midterm elections.

His deeply unpopular war of choice with Iran and its impact on already widespread unaffordability have put Democrats tearing ahead in races across the country and turned many previously safe Republican seats competitive for the first time in decades. 

Pollsters are now forecasting that a Democratic lead of more than 9 points on the generic congressional ballot could hand them control of the House and possibly even the Senate.

Enten’s breakdown on Thursday of the expected bloodbath began in Texas, where the network’s numbers show scandal-ridden GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton trailing Democratic rising star James Talarico by 6 points. 

“I went through the record books at this late stage of the campaign to try and find any Democratic Senate nominee who was up by as much as James Talarico,” he said.

“To find that, you have to go all the way back to 1988,” he added. 

The data guru then noted that Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in Kansas in almost a century and that the party’s nominee Adam Hamilton is now polling at 49 percent.

Enten called it “the Democrats’ best Kansas Senate poll in 30-plus years” and said it means a state “that has been ruby-red for a long time” could “actually finally turn blue.”

The Daily Beast has contacted the Republican National Committee for comment on this story.

news.title: I’m a gen Z voter. Content creators have far less power than politicians think | Alex Bronzini-Vender
news.text:
In tight races, any group that shifts a few points can be called decisive. In 2024, however, gen Z voters actually earned the spotlight.

Take Michigan, where Donald Trump won by about 1.4 points: he and Kamala Harris evenly split the youth vote, a 24-point collapse in the Democratic edge since 2020. If young voters made up just 15% of the state’s electorate, their swing toward the president would be worth roughly 3.6 points, larger than Trump’s entire margin of victory.

Ever since, both parties have scrambled to court the tastemakers who seem to have gen Z’s ear.

At her debut briefing, the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt reserved a “new media seat” in the briefing room, inviting podcasters, influencers and content creators to apply for credentials. The NRCC, House Republicans’ campaign arm, has paid more than $120,000 to a network of conservative influencers, listing the expense simply as “media”.

Not to be outdone, the Democratic National Committee has partnered with more than 500 online personalities through its “Influencer & Creative” operation – and has lately floated the idea of a creator-hosted debate during the 2028 primaries.

The same wishful theory undergirds all these efforts: both parties seem to think online creators can simply upload political opinions straight into our heads.

As a zoomer myself, I find this theory rather patronizing. More to the point, it isn’t true: there’s little evidence that online creators play much of a role in how zoomers actually vote. And if young voters decide these midterms, influencers shouldn’t get the credit.

Plenty of people watch influencers, but very few people deeply trust them.

In a survey this year by the Media Insight Project, 63% of 18-to-34-year-olds said they get news from influencers “at least sometimes”. Yet among teens and adults who actually receive news from these people, just 9% report having a great deal of confidence in what they are being told. (AI chatbots enjoy a nearly identical rate of trust, at 10%.)

Other polls have found much the same thing: when YouGov surveyed young voters across eight battleground states in September on whom they actually turn to for political advice, half named a family member and three in 10 named a friend. Just 6% named an influencer.

In another survey of young people released this spring by Circle, a civic-engagement research center at Tufts, just 9% of respondents said they got political information from social media posts by influencers and celebrities. Another 14% pointed to podcasts hosted by influencers, artists, comedians or other celebrities.

By contrast, 45% of respondents – the largest share – got their information from political, advocacy or community organizations they follow, while nearly a third cited conversations with family and friends.

To whatever extent that internet personalities actually persuade people, their powers rest entirely on the illusion that they speak for themselves. Naturally, both parties have responded by shattering that illusion.

Campaigns and their allies increasingly pay for those voices, often at exorbitant prices. In this year’s race for California governor, Tom Steyer paid at least 17 influencers $5,000 or more apiece, while Katie Porter’s campaign paid one lifestyle creator $25,000 for what appeared to be a single post. A TikTok creator with 1.7 million followers said a Republican-affiliated group had offered her $36,000 for a video, and a company with deep Republican ties once paid a squad of gen Z creators to defend Ken Paxton, now Texas’s Republican Senate nominee, on X.

Some influencers attempt to keep these “partnerships” hidden. The New York Times found that Josh Greene, a progressive creator with nearly 800,000 followers, had not always disclosed the fact that he’d taken money from at least seven candidates and allied groups this cycle.

And when the payments do come to light – as they tend to – they risk destroying the very credibility that campaigns were trying to buy. As the Rainey Center for Public Policy found this summer, 47% of voters said they’d trust a creator less after learning a political post had been paid for by a campaign; only 11% said they’d trust them more.

Obviously, the internet matters. Zohran Mamdani, who won young men by roughly 40 points in last year’s New York mayoral race, has said many New Yorkers he met knew him only from his appearances on podcasts such as Flagrant, hosted by the comedian Andrew Schulz. (As Mamdani put it, Democrats should “stop treating young people and young men with the condescension that we often see and hear in our politics”.) And Trump’s tour of the podcasting sphere in 2024 had racked up more than 100m YouTube views by the day after the election that year.

Still, both appearances were interviews, not simply paid content. Even if the questioning is friendly, the candidates still do most of the talking. And the podcast-interview format itself isn’t magic: Kamala Harris’s appearance on Call Her Daddy seems to have done little to move young voters.

Every older generation finds the next one inscrutable, and gen Z is an especially tough read. Older Americans can be forgiven for struggling to grasp what it means to come of age in the era of social media. (Our memes are, admittedly, really weird.)

Still, if you ignore our screen time, we’re pretty normal after all. Like swing voters twice our age, we’ve ditched the Republican party because prices remain stubbornly high. For all the money Washington is spending to decode our political decision-making, the most surprising thing about gen Z voters may be just how boringly ordinary we are.

 Alex Bronzini-Vender is a writer living in New York
news.summary:
Both US parties scramble to win young voters via influencer operations. The evidence doesn’t support their efforts

In tight races, any group that shifts a few points can be called decisive. In 2024, however, gen Z voters actually earned the spotlight.

Take Michigan, where Donald Trump won by about 1.4 points: he and Kamala Harris evenly split the youth vote, a 24-point collapse in the Democratic edge since 2020. If young voters made up just 15% of the state’s electorate, their swing toward the president would be worth roughly 3.6 points, larger than Trump’s entire margin of victory.
